On the motion of Sir Robert Borden for Committee of Supply:

The motion of the hon. member for Kamouraska is an amendment to the motion that I do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Supply. This amendment contains certain declarations in the nature of a preamble, and asks the House, for certain reasons, to respectfully suggest to a Provincial Legislative Assembly the wisdom of a course of action recommended by the general tenor of the amendment. A point of order has been raised that this amendment is not in order because the subject matter of the amendment is not within the jurisdiction of this Parliament.
It is the duty of your Speaker to enforce, and, subject to your instructions, to administer and interpret the rules and practice enacted and prescribed by your House for the orderly conduct of its business and debates; but the privileges, powers and jurisdiction of the House are matters of the very greatest importance and must be determined by the House itself.

A motion to go into Committee of Supply is parliamentarily of a different nature from other motions in that debate upon it need not be relevant to the motion before the House. Almost any matter can be discussed on the main motion itself. There are, indeed, a few limitations of a strictly technical nature which need not be referred to here (See Bourinot, 3rd ed., p. 585). The present amendment is one asking for an expression of opinion on the part of the House upon a matter of general public interest and need not be relevant nor upon a subject within the legislative powers of this House. As to the nature of amendments which may be made at such a time, May (5th ed., p. 554) says:
The ancient constitutional doctrine, that the redress of grievances is to be considered before the granting of Supply, is now represented by the practice of permitting every description of amendment to be moved on the question for the Spea'ker' leaving the Chair before going into the Committee of Supply. Upon other orders of the day such amendments must be relevant, but here they are permitted to relate to every question upon which any member may desire to offer a motion.
Bourinot, 3rd ed., on page 583, quotes these observations with approval, and adds:
The same practice is now followed very extensively in the Canadian Commons.
He cites in support of this statement many pages of the Journals of the House. Bourinot refers to certain limitations of this right, such as that only one amendment may be moved .at a time, but he nowhere suggests that sueh an amendment would be inadmissible because the subject matter was beyond the legislative jurisdiction of the House.
The Journals are replete with instances of amendments of almost every description on going into Supply. These have been debated and voted upon without objection on the grounds either of relevancy or want of jurisdiction.
Members of this House, being here to act in the interest of all Canada, I think it is proper that any of them may bring before it, on the motion to go into Supply, any matter which in his opinion may be detrimental or advantageous to any section of the population.
In my opinion, the point of order is not well taken. By ruling that this amendment is in order, I mean that this House has the right to discuss it, not with the view of depriving a province of what may have been enacted by its legislature, but merely with the view of,,allowing the House to express its opinion.
Mr. W. B. NOKTHRUP (East Hastings) appealed from the ruling of Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I feel it to be my imperative duty to move this resolution and to invite the discussion of this subject, which is of the utmost importance for the welfare of this country. I assure the right hon. the Prime Minister, for whom I have the greatest respect, that, previous to his appeal of yesterday, I had given to this matter the most earnest and serious consideration. I knew that the course which I had adopted would be disagreeable to many and that I would receive remonstrances and even castigations. For the last few weeks we have been cautioned and warned against approaching this subject in the Dominion Parliament on account of its extreme gravity, lest it should lead to further and more acute dissension between the two gtreat races which compose the majority of the Canadian people. But ignoring difficulties, ignoring problems, is not solving them. On the contrary, I believe it is our duty, as the national representatives of the whole of Canada, to deal with the subject which is embodied in the resolution which I have the honour to move. This question, from its nature, has become a national question. We cannot ignore it. We have to treat it courageously and patriotically. There is no question which affects vitally one section of this country which does not affect the others; especially is that the case when it relates to the language which one-third of the population of this country claim as their birthright.
I earnestly hope that this discussion, instead of being a cause of discord, will promote a better understanding and a closer union between the two races. I do not want to create any ill-feeling, although unfortunately that exists at the present time. I do not want to accentuate any ill-feeling that exists; my purpose is to dispel it. During the last two years Mr. Lloyd George has pleaded in Great Britain for peace at home. That is what we need in Canada also.
It is a coincidence of good omen that tihis House should be the first assembly in the British Empire to be called upon to endorse

and give effect in some way to the wish formulated in the resolution adopted unanimously on the 10th of April last by the British and French inter-parliamentary delegates at the meeting held in London on that date. The resolution, which I haw taken from the London Times, reads:
Believing that the alliance between the French and English peoples will be cemented by a more thorough knowledge on the part of each people of the mind and the literature of the other, the Franco-British Interparliamentary Committee expresses its conviction that the teaching and spelling of the French and the English languages respectively should be, as far as possible, encouraged and developed in both countries, and it commends this subject to the prompt and earnest consideration of the educational authorities and of the teachers in France and in the United Kingdom.
The mover of this resolution, Mr. Franklin Bouillon, gave an interview to the Daily Chronicle, and I take it from the edition of that newspaper of April 11, 1916:
We think that no solid union can be built up except by the mutual interpretation of mind, said Mr. Franklin Bouillon, referring to the question of the teaching of the English and Franch languages which he had introduced at the conference. That was the only way to bind the two peoples together. The feeling of the whole conference was that such a consummation was absolutely to be desired, and our duty, after what we had learned, was that we the dominions and countries united, should be prepared to make an arrangement in future so that we should be perfectly independent economically Just as we have been and would re- . main politically.
Lord Bryce was the president of the conference, and the resolution, which was carried unanimously, was moved by Mr. Franklin Bouillon and seconded by Sir Henry Craik, M.P.
I said that it was a rather fortunate circumstance that this Canadian Parliament should be the first to be called upon to endorse this resolution of the representatives of the Allied countries, and it is quite appropriate that such should be the case. This Parliament is the greatest bilingual institution in the British Empire, and it is but natural that we should view with favour and approval this new and most fortunate course adopted by,the representative leaders of our two great mother countries.
The Canadian Confederation was a compromise. It is certainly to be regretted that periodically questions arise that endanger the work of unity and national harmony which is so essential to the building up and development of a great country. Such questions cannot be avoided;

but it is the duty of Canadian public men to approach and to deal with them in a spirit of tolerance, justice, and liberty. It is impossible to prevent those troublesome questions from beingf thrown into the political arena; but surely, after fifty years of Confederation, the two branches of the Canadian family must have come of age; they must be able to put aside the fanatics and the demagogues; they must be able to adjust their difficulties and to settle their controversies in that most commendable spirit described by Lincoln: "With malice toward none; with charity for all." Our social fabric is based entirely upon the mutual respect of the rights of the two great Canadian races. This principle is at the very root of our constitution. It is necessary for those who are not familiar with the history of this country that they should be made acquainted with' that fact. There is no place in Canada for narrowness of mind or prejudice; indeed, there should be no place for them in any country in the world. Moderation, tolerance, and charity must be the governing principles of all creeds, races, and colours, and the Golden Kule should apply to all.
I do not purpose dealing with the legal and constitutional aspect of the question, although I may refer to it incidentally for the purpose of my argument. This resolution does not recommend the disallowance of any of the provincial laws of Ontario. It does not imply any blame or censure upon the course adopted by the Government in dealing with the petitions praying for the disallowance of that legislation. Indeed, I personally believe that disallowance would have been unwise; the Temedy might, perhaps, have increased the disease. Coercion of any kind will not settle the difficulties. I am a true Liberal and a believer in provincial lights. I will go so far as to admit that to be effective and successful any final settlement of this question must be made in Ontario and by Ontario herself. But, Sir, is it not the right of this Parliament, while declining to interfere with the provincial legislation of Ontario by the exercise of the power of disallowance or otherwise, to appeal to the rulers of that province for a generous and peaceful settlement of this disturbing question and for a redress of the grievances of the minority? If the majority would not accept coercion on the part of this Parliament with regard to what they consider to be their provincial rights, how can they
expect that the minority will tamely submit to coercion on the part of the provincial Legislature with regard to what the members of the minority also consider to be their most sacred and inalienable rights? Is it not our duty as representatives of the great Canadian family to plead with this member of that family, to ask him who is the big brother to be fair to his little and weaker brother, to be generous with him, to help him along in his struggles and not to quarrel with him? Surely, this is not coercion.
Sir, the French Canadians of Ontario love their language. We all love it. W,e love it because it is our own language. Let any hon. gentleman, let any man, consult his own personal feeling; let him consult his own heart and he will realize how great ds his affection for the language that he learned to speak on the knees of his mother. But we love the French language also because we sincerely feel that it is the sweetest and purest and noblest language which has ever been spoken by human lips. We love it because of its great literature. We love it for its glorious history. We love it because of 3 p.m. its clearness, which is so great that a German author is reported to have said: " I am anxious to have my book translated into French in order to understand it better." French, in the words of John Quincy Adams, is the acknowledged neutral language of all refined society; it is the language of diplomacy; its influence is world-wide. The reports of French literary statistics show that one-half of every edition of a French novel is sold outside of France, and that two-thirds of .the more serious works are sold in foreign countries. Take the case of my hon. friend the member for Wright (Mr. E. B. Devlin), the seconder of this resolution. My hon. friend is an Irishman who has not a drop of French blood an his veins. Where did he acquire that knowledge and mastery of the French language which he possesses? He acquired it in a college in Great Britain. Let me give an illustration of the real status of the French language in the world. I will quote an article entitled, " French spoken in Berlin," from La Gazette de Lausanne:
While Berlin is zealously striving to expunge from the German language all those grossly deformed and mutilated terms which they had originally borrowed from ours, French victoriously makes its entry into the capital of the Empire via Constantinople. A Bernese newspaperman who is a friend of ours, returning from a trip to Germany, states

liament of Canada and are entitled as a right to stand up in this Parliament and address you, Mr. Speaker, in the French language. It is not fair to contend that in order to exercise what is their right, they must have the privilege of receiving in the schools of the country, which they maintain with their own money, the education which will enable them to do so. But the advocates of By-law 17 claim that they do not want' to prevent the teaching of the French language, that their only purpose is to improve the methods and quality of bilingual education, and that their regulations have been enacted for the advantage and benefit of the French-speaking children. Sir, the sense of fairness is so deeply rooted in the mind of the average English-speaking Canadian that to induce him to accept' a wrong or an injustice, some moral excuse or justification must be given for that wrong. The wolf will always find some pretence to justify his eating of the lam'b. I assure you that this sort of benevolent despotism does not appeal to me. I acknowledge the good faith of many of those who support and defend these regulations. I believe that the greater number of them would refuse to endorse the proscription of the language which is the pride of so many of their fellow citizens. But there is not the slightest doubt in my mind, and there is not the slightest doubt in the mind of any one .who has received even a smattering of French education that these regulations, although they proceed more slowly, proceed obliquely, and more insidiously perhaps, but with no less certainty to the same end, namely, the strangling of the French tongue.
The time at my disposal does not permit me to analyse any of these regulations, nor do I think that this is the proper place to do so. Allow me to point out, however, that what is left of the study of French can only be made in the schools which were in operation and in which French was a subject of study previous to 1912. Does not that seem an unpatriotic reservation? It is inflicting a penalty upon the French-Cana-dians for being guilty of observing too well the law of multiplication prescribed by the Almighty. It is an inducement to race suicide. I believe, however, that the moral character and temperament of my countrymen will successfully resist any such unpatriotic design.
Another feature of the regulations which is also absolutely unacceptable is that no teaching of French shall be given in any manner except with the consent and on
fMr. E. Lapointe.]
the approval of the inspector, from whose decision there is no appeal. I cannot understand why such a condition of things should receive the approval of any fair-minded man. My idea of what constitutes liberty _ precludes me from admitting that it can be sufficiently preserved when the citizen must depend upon the benevolence, the whim, or, in some cases, perhaps upon the prejudices of a minister, or any of his servants. Surely that is not liberty. For my part I cannot help thinking that these regulations were an unfortunate wounding of the French Canadians of Ontario in their deepest and most permanent susceptibilities. They have resented it, and their countrymen of the same race and language have resented it as well, and we have been passing through a serious crisis which threatens to become still more acute. But what to my mind is the most deplorable feature of the situation is not the agitation which has developed; there is something graver than the abuses and violences of language. What is peculiarly painful is that this unholy war is being waged at the expense of the most sacred and innocent victim; at the expense of the child. The Canadian children ought to ignore our conflicts and our rivalries. They ought to live in an atmosphere of peace and order. Is it not to be regretted that in the blood of these children should be instilled the poison of old hatreds and antipathies. We need greater things in this country. As to the proscription of the French language in Ontario, I have no fear whatever. A coercive policy will never assimilate a race, nor proscribe a language. That is a truism of sociology which all the governments of the world ought to remember. Will you permit me to read in that connection an article by Emile Faguet, a member of the French Academy, on the recent proscription of the French language in Bulgaria, after that country had joined Germany against the Allies:
The Czar Ferdinand of Bulgaria has just forbidden in his kingdom the use of the French language. The fact strikes one as strange, even in a period of extraordinary happenings.
What can be the matter with that czar? As far as blood goes, he is a half-Frenchman. He is a grandson of the first and last " king of the French." He has received a French education. What then ails him, and, as the poet said: Against all his past history turns him on a sudden?
What harm has the French language done him? It is up to this day the instrument of diplomacy, and should we infer that the Czar Ferdinand has made up his mind that none of his subjects will take up the profession in which Talleyrand made a name for himself?

That would be taking a rather narrow view of the situation.
However, if such is not his purpose, such is the direct outcome of his action. A queer departure, indeed.
Would it be, perchance, that the French language is tainted and carries with it some deadly germ which it transmits to whoever uses it or tries to learn it? I wonder what it can be. It supplies a clear, systematic, direct means of expression, which enables one to speak to the point, without circumlocutions or roundabout verbosity; besides, a straightforward means of expression, which to those who make use of it can impart nothing but a liking for loyalty and honesty. Who is it fears such an infection? Who will acknowledge that he fears it? Who will allow such a suspicion to rest on himself? No living man. Well, then, why does the Czar of Bulgaria act as if he feared the natural play of the use of that tongue on those who make use of it? That is absolutely beyond comprehension.
There is no one-and that is a fact more especially as regards rulers of people-who is not desirous that his subordinates, his dependents, his subjects, should be above all true and honest. AH then should see to it that those over whom they hold sway learn French with all their heart and speak it fluently. The following anecdote is familiar to a good many: Louis the Fourteenth advised one of his courtiers to learn Spanish, and the latter, surmising that the king destined him to be ambassador at the court of Spain, forthwith set himself to the task but was sorely disappointed when on returning to the king with the news that he could now speak the Spanish language, was simply told: Very well, then I think you would enjoy reading Don Quixote in the original. Similarly, instead of a ruler forbidding the use of French by his people, I would fancy one inquiring from some of his courtiers: Do you know French?-No.-Well, learn it, that will impart to you notions of righteousness in every form.
Ferdinand of Bulgaria is doing exactly the opposite. It cannot be gainsaid, he acts strangely. He has reasons with very little reason in them, and which, besides, are not prompted by any kindheartedness.
I can perceive only one motive which may have had some bearing on the resolve taken by the Czar of Bulgaria. He has been jeered and to a certain extent discussed in French. It must be admitted that he has been somewhat ill-used in French. But, your Majesty, is that a reason? Is there any sense in prohibiting the use of a whole literature from Villon to Rostand, just because some of those who speak the language have used it to banter you? That is trying to get even with a vengeance.
How touchy the victim, and how magnifying and long-armed his desire for revenge! What! shall a language be proscribed as a whole on account of a few words in that language which have displeased you, and which, I aver, had) not been said for the purpose of conciliating you. A whole tongue put under ban on account of a few sounds which have grated on yours ears! That is exactly the stand taken by Aman in Racine's play, Esther:
" Un seul osa d'Aman attirer le courroux: Aussitdt de la terre ils disparurent tous."
And that stand has always been held to smack of megalomania. A language as a
whole cannot be proscribed, not any more than a people as a whole. Of course, that may be done theoretically, but by no means actually. Bulgarians will continue to learn French, with this added peculiarity that henceforth that tongue will have the further allurement of the forbidden fruit. Czar Ferdinand, in emitting that decree, has simply conferred on the French language a wider popularity, and that popularity will only increase in range and intensity as generations go by. Nothing is as effective as proscription towards furthering that end. Young Bulgarians will say to one another:
You know, that is the language which Czar Ferdinand intended to behead.*'
Sir, the present time is one when all sources of trouble and division ought to be removed. Canada is in urgent need of the union of her citizens. All moderate and welbmeaning men of the country must regard it as a pity that tihe schools of the capital city of Ottawa should be closed, and that thousands of school children should parade the streets while the fathers and brothers of many of them are fighting and dying for liberty in the trenches of France and Belgium. Is it not to be deplored that such a fight about the French language should take place when France and Britain have formed a glorious and indissoluble union for the good of the world and the great cause of civilization? There is no longer a channel between the peoples of Great Britain and of France. Why should there be one in this country between their descendants? I have referred to the resolution adopted by the Franco-Britisib parliamentary delegates on the 10th April last. Those delegates met first in France, at Paris and at Bordeaux. The first conference was presided over by Mr. George Clemenoeau, a former Prime Minister of France, and he was entrusted with the agreeable duty of welcoming the British delegates. I happened one afternoon, in the Teading room of this House, to read some beautiful and inspiring extracts from his speech. I fear that I have already detained the House too long, but if the House will bear with me I will give a few passages from this speech, which, as hon. gentlemen will perceive, are of a high literary order:
To the members of the British committee:
Gentlemen, we wish you a hearty welcome; and may the man who owes it to his advancing years to address you in the name of his colleagues of the French parliamentary committee, be allowed to tell you that, even in the darkest days, he never despaired of the concluding of an entente which appeared to him bound to materialize some day, though he had lost hope of seeing it effected during his lifetime.
Yes, gentlemen, X have been expecting you for endless jenturie^; and historians, who too often are out of touch with those undercurrents

of love and hatred which alternate in the lives of people, may express surprise at the length of time it took for us to join hands across such a narrow expanse of sea; an impassable barrier, if viewed in the light of so many adventurous war undertakings, but which is now in our eyes a great highway open to all who are worthy of comprehending and practising the future true brotherhood of nations, founded on a recognition of the equal rights of all and the proper consideration of the right of every one.
Yes, T repeat it, I have been expecting j'ou since Hastings,, since the days of the Black Prince. You may judge how persistent I am.
I was awaiting you, and you have come, and here you are the representatives of the English people who, of your own impulse, have crossed the Channel, not to conclude a political agreement-our respective governments will see to lhat. neither is it to investigate military tactics, a subject which is necessarily outside our purview.
No. your visit is something like the forecasted crowning of all these labours. We are meeting simply for the purpose of seeing one another, of understanding one another, and of finding ourselves capable of loving one another. The present time requires action, and civilians as well as the military, on both sides of the Chan- ' nel are engaged in action and will remain so, whatever the outcome, until the end. Until the end. do you catch my meaning?
With all the authority with which he is clothed, Lord Desart made that final statement. Our minds are made up, our purpose is set, our honour is pledged. We are giving our children, we will give our wealth, everything, everything, and such is the reward that may be expected from the triumph of the lofty cause of the independence of nations and the dignity of man, that despite the most heart-rending sacrifices, we shall never complain that we had to give too much.
Such is the great international secret which has led you across the seas to come to us. . .
True it is that to the war is due the miracle of a deep mutual understanding, which now could not be broken without calamity to civilization. We did not seek war, neither your nation nor our nation, and now we are both bent on having it, and so our good allies; and we are earnest about it, and we will have it as long as may be necessary to reach a complete victory-complete, do you hear?-that will repay us and repay our brave sons for those torrents of blood, such torrents as have never drenched any country in history. . . Heart to heart, as our soldiers are doing side by side, we shall live in a great bond of union, that no frenzy of hatred must ever tear asunder, and together we shall have accomplished something which short-sighted minds will perhaps deem insignificant because made without any display of pomp, but which nevertheless will mark an epoch in the forward march of humanity.
M. Paul Deschanel, President of the Chamber of Deputies in France, said:
Never was bond more necessary. The genius of Great Britain and that of France complete, impregnate and magnetize each other. Both bend themselves with a remarkable suppleness to the unforeseen exigencies of the most terrible of all wars. Together they come to the rescue of civilization now threatened with a frightful return to savagery; together, along-

side our dear and brave allies, they will save the honour of mankind. Long live England and long live France, forever united in the triumph of justice.
But, Sir, immediately after having read these fine words, expressive of union and amity, my attention was called to an article published in an important newspaper of Ontario, the London Free Press, on March 4, 1916, and entitled "A Quebec Plot," I quote the following sentence from it:
The Liberal leader in Ontario must cease this practice of speaking to French audiences in Ontario in the French tongue.
This sentence would have made a most painful impression on me if I had not believed then, as I believe now, that this newspaper was not representing the true sentiments of my English-speaking fellow citizens.
In closing my remarks, I trust that in dealing with this delicate subject I have not offended the feelings of any hon. gentleman in this House. I have only done what I deemed to be my imperative duty. My most earnest desire is that this resolution and this debate, instead of driving our two great races further asunder, will contribute to weld them more indissolubly together in the defence of liberty under the law. I ask my fellow members to proclaim with Gladstone, the equality of the weak with the strong. It is our most difficult task to unite and reconcile the nation. We must inspire Canadian public life with a lofty and courageous spirit; we must protect the equal rights of all the citizens; and above all, erect in this Canadian land a strong and solid wall against the mad blows of violence and prejudice. To reach that end, we must ask our fellow-citizens to make concessions, to be compliant, to bear with each other and respect each other's opinions. I hope that in this way we shall succeed in creating that harmony which is as necessary to the welfare of the State as it is to the welfare of individuals.

Mr. Speaker, listening to the prayer with which we open our daily proceedings in this House, the words " May peace and harmony always reign among us," appealed to me as they always have since I have had the honour of a seat in this House, and I trust that the temper and spirit of my words this afternoon will not in any way be in discord with that pious supplication. The resolution which is now

before the House is divided into three distinct parts. It has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite that it is a great pity that this resolution ever came up in this House. Might I say at once that I have that feeling myself. I think it is unfortunate that legislation should be passed by any province -which would so affect the sensibilities of a great minority in this country as to force them to apply to this House for redress. Nevertheless, certain legislation, to which I shall refer, has been passed by the Legislature of Ontario. Petitions have come to this House, applications have been made to the representatives of the people to bring this question before the Canadian public through the Federal Parliament; speeches have been delivered from the public platform; I take it that all these are an appeal on behalf of the French minority in this country, not for the disallowance of any Act which has been passed by the Ontario or any other Legislature, but an appeal to the intelligence, to the judgment, and to the generosity of the Canadian people. I am a Canadian. I believe in the most absolute freedom and liberty for the people of all races and of all creeds in this country. Whenever I hear or read noble sentiments appealing to the generosity of the people of my country, I am forced to applaud. When I read a short time ago the speeches delivered by the right hon. the Prime Minister of this country in England, I felt that he was representing the true sentiments of the Canadian people. Will you, Sir, allow me to quote some words which the right hon. gentleman uttered in a speech at the town hall in Bristol, England, on August 10, 1915:
Throughout this Empire we have many races and many creeds; but all united by a single purpose at this juncture. So we In Canada are not all of one race. Those who-came first to the soil of Canada were of a great nation, now happily an Ally of ours, the great French nation. There are to-day within these islands, at Shorncliffe, several regiments whose mother-tongue is French, and not English, who have come from Canada to do their part in the great struggle. In the development of constitutional government in Canada-which has Indeed proceeded very much on the same lines as with you -Canadians of French descent have laboured harmoniously and effectively with us whose forefathers came from these islands. And no better exponents of the cause of constitutional government and liberty in Canada have been found than these descended from the first pioneer race of Canda, the French race. We in Canada find the need, realized everywhere throughout the Empire, that we should know and understand each other a little better. In a vast country like ours, with scattered communities, diverse in race, diverse in creed, and sometimes
in ideal and apparent interest, there is the greatest need of mutual understanding and comprehension. And as we have come to know ourselves better during the past twenty-five or fifty years, so the national spirit of Canada has been awakened, and has become strong and vigorous.
Those sentiments ought to be applauded throughout Canada as I feel they must have been applauded in Great Britain. Might I be allowed to make a further quotation from another speech of the right hon. the Prime Minister, delivered in the Guild Hall, London, England, on July 29, 1915:
While it may not be fitting that one of our kindred should speak of the British people as a great race, nevertheless, I may at least say that it has wrought great things. And the greatest of all its achievements is the upbuilding of an Empire sustained by ties such as those which unite ours. In the beginning, the founding of a nation within these islands, and the consequent necessity of orderly government, compelled a system autocratic in its character and methods. Then came the great charters of freedom and the will of the people to make their own laws and govern themselves. Orderly government on the one hand; indivi-vidual liberty on the other; justice, the -equality of all men before the law-upon these secure foundations the fabric of the national life was built; and in these later years there has come the not less noble ideal of a democracy founded upon equality of opportunity for all the people. . .
And Wily are the descendants in Canada of those who fought under Wolfe and of those who fought under Montcalm wlien contending for the possession of the northern half of the American continent, why are they now standing together in the Empire's battle line? To speak of later events, why do we find beyond the channel, in France or in Belgium, the grandson of a Durham and the grandson of a Papineau standing side by side in this struggle? When the historian of the future comes to analyse the events of this war, he will realize that some great overmastering impulse contributed mainly to this wonderful result. One such impulse is to be found in the love of liberty, the ideals of democracy, and the spirit of unity founded thereon, which make the whole Empire one in aim and purpose.
When I first read those words, my thoughts reverted at once to the celebration in 1908 of the Tercentenary of the foundation of Quebec and of the marvellous gathering of representatives of the component parts of the British Empire, and to the expressions, uttered in the presence of His Majesty the King, by eminent men of our Dominion, of their profound loyalty and attachment to the Throne, the flag and the free institutions governing this country and the Empire. Those sentiments were echoed by every one in every province in Canada. Canada was there represented as a Dominion; the narrow confines of provincialism

were forgotten, and men of the French race and men of the English race, grouped around the monument of Samuel de Champlain, seemed to form a new monument-a monument to the greatness of the unity of the people of Canada. There were expressions by eminent men of this Dominion as to the unity of the races in this country, as to the ideals which governed us in Canada. Some of those men have passed .away; some are still living. Let me refer you, Sir, to the opening remarks of the mayor of the city of Quebec at fhat time, Sir George Garneau:
The French-Canadians experience an inexpressible feeling of patriotic pride and gratitude towards the two great nations who have in turn presided over our destinies: France, always beloved, to whom they owe their life and noble traditions; England, who left them free to grow up keeping their faith, their language and their institutions, and who endowed them with a constitutional government based upon the largest amount of liberties, and which is undeniably the noblest and most perfect in the world.
Therein, in my humble judgment, is the teal feeling of a French Canadian. He is attached to France because from France he got life; from France he got his great traditions. He is attached to England because England has allowed him to grow up in his faith, in his language, and in his institutions, and because England has given to this country a constitutional Government founded upon the greatest sum of liberty, which is, as Sir George Garneau puts it, "the best and most perfect in the world."
The only other expression which I would like to give to the Mouse is of one who has passed away, Sir James Whitney, who, speaking upon the same occasion, said:
We, Sir, of the other provinces, respect and
love our fellow subjects of Quebec for their intrinsic worth and for their attitude and aid in times of stress and peril. We cannot forget the answer sent when they were urged to join hands with a foreign power against the British Empire.
We cannot forget Chateauguay, where the gallant de Salaberry performed the most scientific military feat of the war of 1812.
Sir, within a mile of my birthplace, on the historic field of Chrysler's farm, was done what Sir Nigel Boring would term a "comfortable feat of arms."
And we cannot forget that there and then a company of French Canadian voltigeurs reddened the soil of Upper Canada with their blood in. defence of British institutions and British connections.
Nor can we forget the memorable words of Sir Etienne Tachfi, when he declared that " the last shot fired in Canada in defence of British connections will be fired by a French Canadian."

Sir, we could not forget these things if we would, and on behalf of the provinces, I make bold to say also that we would not forget them if we could. We revere the memories of the great men of Quebec, of Tachg and Dafontaine, of Morin and Cartier, Chapleau and Dorion, among the dead and offer our tribute of respect and honour to Laurier among the living.
Those are the words which have been uttered by some of the great men of this country; those are the sentiments which I understand actuate every true Canadian, and in harmony with those sentiments I shall briefly deal with the resolution which I have had the honour of seconding. The first part of the resolution reads:
It has long been the settled policy of Great Britain whenever a country passed under the sovereignty of the Crown by treaty or otherwise, to respect the religion, the usages and the language of the inhabitants who thus become British subjects.
Referring solely to our own country, we find that that was exactly the policy which was carried put by Great Britain, because, if you refer to the third article of the Capitulation of this country, you will find:
That the inhabitants shall be preserved in the possession of their houses, goods, effects and privileges.
That article was granted upon the condition of the inhabitants laying down their arms. Later on in 1774, Sir James Marriott, then Advocate General, was asked to report to the King upon certain conditions existing in this country, and, amongst other things, upon that very article, and his report is contained in the following words:
The treaty made with the sovereign power of France, which, without taking notice of the capitulation transfers its subjects pleno jure, does not supersede the capitulation made with the inhabitants; because I consider capitulations, in the eye of the law of nations, to be not only as national, but personal compacts, and made with the inhabitants themselves, for the consideration of their ceasing their existence. It is consistent with the honour and interests of this Kingdom, that they should be religiously observed, and that the condition of the grantee should be rendered substantially better, rather than worse, so far as any person or persons are capable of taking benefit of the grant.
Since that time there have been several Acts passed by the Imperial Government concerning the constitution of our country. There was the Quebec Act of 1774, in which the principle was again laid down; there was the Constitutional Act of 1791; there was the Union Act of 1840, none of which Acts affected the use of the French language throughout the Dominion of Canada.

A.gain, there was the Confederation Act of 1867. The only section of that Act which deals with the nse of the Frer.cn language is section 133, which places both languages in the same footing in this Parliament, in the courts of this (Dominion, and in the courts and legislature of the province of Quebec. Since the legislation of 1867 permits the French language, to be an official language of this country-and you cannot in this Parliament oi in any legislature take away that right-is it the part of w.sdom to allow the children to use that , language on the streets of any village, town or city in Ontario, or in any part of that or any other province, and yet not give them the right to learn how to speak that language correctly? I may be wrong, but in my humble judgment, Sir, it is elementary logic that if by your legislation you provide that a language shall be official in your country, it naturally follows that you must give to the users of that language the opportunity of learning it.
The principle of the recognition by Great Britain of the right to the use of other languages than the English language has been referred to by the hon. member for Kam-ouraska. I find also that under the British Nationality and Status of Aliens Act of 1914, persons naturalized prior to January 1, 1915, may after that date apply for a fresh certificate of naturalization under new conditions; and, in order to be eligible for such certificate in the United Kingdom an alien must amongst other things be of good character and have an adequate knowledge of the English language. It does not say that he must have a thorough possession of the English language, that he must know the English language and that only; it says that he must have an adequate knowledge of the English language. In our country, by our Naturalization Act, he may know either the French or the English language. That law, passed by this Parliament quite recently, gives every French Canadian in this country, no matter into what province he wants to go, the right to use only the French language if he will. If the law is good, if it is sound, if it is based upon logic, is it the part of wisdom to prevent the children of these people, coming into this country and having the right to the use of that language, from learning how to speak the French language correctly?
The second part of the resolution is:
That His Majesty's subjects of French origin in the province of Ontario complain that by recent legislation they have been to a large extent deprived of the privileges which they and their fathers have always enjoyed since Canada passed under the sovereignty of the British Crown, of having their children taught in French.	-
The French Canadians of the province of Ontario claim that they have a grievance. They have, as I said in the beginning of my remarks, petitioned the Government; they have through their press and from the public platform told us that they have a grievance. They ask us as their representatives to bring that grievance before the Canadian Parliament, and to appeal to its judgment and its intelligence.' For a moment I should like to put be-
4 p.m. fore the House what the status of the French Canadians was prior to and since Confederation, and I want to do it, not in my own language, hut in the language of a gentleman who has written a work entitled: "Legislation and History of Separate Schools in Upper Canada, 1841 to 1876," who cannot be said to have any prejudice whatever in the matter. I refer to the work of Mr. George Hodgins, M.A., LL.D., F.R.G.S., barrister-at-law, Librarian of the Education Department for Ontario, and editor of the Documentary History of Education in Upper Canada. The chapter is 33; it is somewhat lengthy, but for the purpose of the argument which I intend making, I should like to read the whole chapter. Mr. Hodgins says:
There was one class of separate schools which gave the chief superintendent very little trouble. These were the French and German schools-chiefly Roman Catholic-which were scattered here and there throughout Upper Canada. All that had to be done in their case was to give them such teaching facilities as enabled them to go into operation under teachers who could speak the language of the ratepayers concerned, and that language only. Happily that faculty could be given under the general, not the separate school law, and that with the sanction of the chief superintendent.
There were two principles which Dr. Ryerson laid down at an early period in his administration of the Education Department. The first was that whenever he could meet special cases by a liberal, and often, with the sanction of the Government, a generous interpretation of his powers under the Schools Acts, and in terms of his commission as chief superintendent of education, it was his duty to give that interpretation in cases not specifically provided for-except by analogy-in the school law. The second principle which Dr. Ryerson laid down, and which he generally adhered to, was not to propose too frequent legislation with a view to meet special cases,

but only to seek such legislation at intervals of from five to ten years. Fortunately I was familiar with Dr. Eyerson's views as expressed in the first of the foregoing principles which he had laid down for his guidance, when the first application was made in 1851 to grant a certificate of qualification to a French teacher in the county of Essex, which had been largely settled by French Canadians. At the time that this application reached me from the Board of Public Instruction for the county of Essex, Dr. Ryerson was absent in England and I had charge of the department as acting chief superintendent. I therefore submitted the application, which had been received, to the Council of Public" Instruction for Upper Canada, with the recommendation that it be granted. This was concurred in by the Council of Public Instruction, and I was therefore, enabled to inform the Essex 'County Board, that:
The Council of Public Instruction for Upper Canada has sanctioned a liberal construction of the programme to which you refer, making the term " English " convertible into the term "French" where it occurs, and when applied to French candidates for examination before the County Board of Public Instruction. The certificate should, of course, be expressly limited to teaching in the French language.
A copy of this intimation was also sent to the then local superintendent of education at Sandwich, with the following addition :
The School Act expressly authorizes trustees to employ any qualified teacher they please; should, therefore, the one to whom you refer obtain a certificate from the County Board, the trustees can engage his services, and no board or school officer can prevent them as has been assumed in a memorial transmitted to me by the secretary of the County Board of Public Instruction, from certain inhabitants of School Seenon No. 6, Sandwich.
In 1858, a partial extension of the principle here laid down was applied to German teachers, and to meet the case a knowledge of the German grammar was by the Council of Public Instruction substituted in the programme of examination for a knowledge of the,English grammar. (Reading):
In 1871 a further difficulty arose owing to a delay of the Council of Public Instruction, to provide fully for the examination and licensing of German teachers in the German settlements of Upper Canada. To meet a special case, which occurred in the county of Waterloo,
I told the local Superintendent, who had called upon me, in Dr. Ryerson's absence:
To grant six months' certificates to such German candidates as would present themselves for examination in July; and I said that, by giving the department early notice of the real requirements in the case, attention would be given to the matter by the Council of Public

Instruction, and every provision made for the examination of such candidates, at all future examinations.	,
This was confirmed by Dr. Ryerson; and he informed the local Superintendent of the county, that examination papers in German reading, spelling, etymology and grammar might be prepared by members of the County Board, and that the other ordinary examination papers could be used in the case of teachers who could read English.
Similar applications, made in 1872 and 1875, were dealt with in the same spirit; and, in this way, every facility w'as given by the Education Department for the successful operation of French and German public and separate schools in the French and German settlements of Upper Canada.
That is further confirmed by a letter which Dr. Ryerson wrote on the 24th of April, 1857, which reads as follows: Gentlemen:
I have the honour to state in reply to your letter of the 16th instant that, as the French is the recognized language of the country, as well as the English, it is quite proper and lawful for the trustees to allow both languages to be taught in their schools to children whose parents may desire them to learn both.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
E. Ryerson.
Therefore, according to Dr. Ryerson's opinion, it was not only proper but lawful for the French language to be taught in the schools of Ontario prior to Confederation. Since Confederation the same right existed down to what is known as Regulation 17. I should like to call attention to a letter which was written by Mr. Col-quhoun, Deputy Minister of Education, on the 24th July, 1911, in which I find these words:
I am directed by the Prime Minister, Sir James Whitney, to acknowledge your letter of the 21st, and to state that no change has been made in the school law of the department regulations affecting the study of the French* language in the schools. I am directed to point out that the question is one entirely under the control of the Board of Trustees.
(Sgd.) A. H. U. Colquhoun.
The only provision respecting education which I find in the British North America Act is the provision contained in section 93, which reads as follows:
In and for each province the Legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education, subject and according to the following provisions :
Nothing in any such law shall prejudicially affect any right or privilege with respect to denominational schools which any class of persons have by law in the province at the Union.
Where in any province a system of separate or dissentient schools exists by law at the Union or is thereafter established by the Legislature of the province, an Appeal shall lie to the Governor-General in Council from any Act or decision of any provincial authority affect-

ing any right or privilege of the Protestant or Roman Catholic minority of the Queen's subjects in relation to education.
Thus, so far, we find that the French language has been tolerated, has been allowed, and has been sanctioned by the laws passed in the province of Ontario. The French Canadians apparently had no grievance whatever until the passing of Regulation 17. But prior to the passing of Regulation 17 another regulation was passed by the Ontario Board which reads as follows:
In school sections where the French or German language prevails, the trustees may, in addition to the course of study prescribed for public schools, require instruction to be given in reading, grammar and composition to such pupils as are directed by their parents or guardians to study either of these languages, and in all such cases the authorized text books in French or German shall be used.
So that by Regulation 15, in the province of Ontario, the French language was sanctioned by the law and the German language was also sanctioned by the law. There was a subsequent resolution passed, regulation 17, which has been greatly spoken of in this country, and under which the French-Cana-dians feel that that they were aggrieved. Regulation 17, in effect proscribes certain privileges which have been accorded to the French Canadians in the use of their language as the language of instruction in their schools. The French Canadians feel that if the Germans are not proscribed in the right to their language in the Ontario schools, the French Canadians should not have their privileges limited. Before Confederation, according to Dr. Ryerson and according to Mr. Hodgins, the Germans and the French Canadians had their full privileges in Ontario. As late as Regulation 15 those privileges were continued and confirmed. By Regulation 17 the language of instruction during the first two years of their instruction may be the French language; but the idea and the spirit and the letter of the law is that the moment they have a sufficient knowledge of the English language, then the French language must be set aside entirely, and their whole education must be conducted along the lines of the English language. The French Canadians claim that they have a grievance. I feel, in my humble judgment, that their grievance is well founded; and, as a Canadian, wishing to see equal justice given to all classes in this community, wishing to see the same justice meted out to the French Canadians as I would want to see meted out to the English-speaking
people, I feel that the second part of this resolution is thoroughly applicable to the circumstances, and therefore I have absolutely no hesitation in agreeing to every letter of it.
The third part of the resolution reads:
That this House especially at this time of universal sacrifice and anxiety, when all energies should be concentrated on the winning of the war, would, while fully recognizing the principle of provincial rights and the necessity of every child being given a thorough English education, respectfully suggest to the Legislative Assembly the wisdom of making it clear that the privilege of the children of French parentage of being taught in their mother tongue be not interfered with.
I would not like to give my own appreciation only of that portion of the resolution which I have seconded, and I would not like the House to be guided solely by my opinion. I refer the House to other opinions to which they might attach, and I have no doubt will attach, a great deal more weight, the opinion of Sir Oliver Mow-at, for instance, in a speech made at Woodstock on December 3, 1889, when he said:
French-Canadians cherish their own language lovingly.
Will you permit me, Mr. Speaker, to in terject a remark and to affirm, as one who knows the French-.Canadian people that their language is part of their soul. They are attached to their language just as they are attached to their faith, to the traditions of this country, and to the British Crown. There is something in their love of their language which may be incomprehensible to those who have not had to do with the French-Canadians, who have not lived among the French-Canadians, and who are not intimately acquainted with them. Sir Oliver Mowat apparently had a thorough appreciation of the French Canadian when he used that language. He goes on:
They wish their children- to love it and be educated in it; but they know it will be for their interest to be familiar with English also, and to be educated in English, as well as French. Proscribe French, their mother tongue, and they will hate you and have nothing to do with your- schools. Permit their own language to receive attention, and they are glad to have their children learn English also as soon and as fast as it can be imparted. Such was the view of the commissioners as to the proper policy; it is the view of this Government ; and it is the view of all intelligent men, except our political opponents. It was the view of Dr. Ryerson and his Council of Public Instruction, even to the extent of putting no pressure whatever on French or German schools, and of awaiting their own spontaneous action as to English and other matters.
There you have the opinion of an English Canadian speakmg in the province of On-

tario. Will you let me quote the opinion of an English Canadian speaking in the province of Quebec only a few days ago before the Canadian Club, the opinion of a man who for years had a seat in the Legislature of Quebec, who has always lived among the French Canadian people, who later became the representative of the English minority in the province of Quebec in the provincial Cabinet, and who later was appointed a judge. I refer to Mr. Justice McCorkill, and I think his words express in better language than I could use the real feeling that animates the province of Quebec in this matter. Speaking on March 28, 1916, he said:
I need not tell you that X have heen a student of Canadian history from the very earliest days. X have read with the greatest interest the history of the old regime, the opening up of the "ountry, and then of the abandonment of the people by their country, so to speak, and of the tremendous efforts they made to keep the country for themselves. I have read the history of the country under the British regime, and how they have fallen in so well with the administration of justice, the administration in our Legislatures and municipalities under the British system. I believe that a certain Prench-Canadian at Ottawa is one of the greatest parliamentarians under the British Constitution that we have in any part of the Empire.
They have adopted our system, but there are two things they have clung to, their religion and their language. I believe that their national sentiment is even stronger than their religious sentiment-I really believe so. The national feeling among them is intensely strong, but I would ask you English, Irish and Scotch descendants born in this country, and brought up here, supposing a regulation similar to No. 17 were passed in the province of Quebec, what do you think our duty towards it would be? Supposing Sir Lomer Gouin-I cannot imagine it- but supposing he did have the courage, or the nerve, so to speak, to pass a regulation of that kind. There would be a rebellion in this province, I think. And here we have our French-Canadian brethren in the sister province who by constitutional means are trying to obtain the repeal or the modification of the regulation, or some other settlement of the question which would be satisfactory to all concerned.
I do not wish, Sir, to delay the business of this House. I have put as concisely as I conveniently can my sentiments upon this question, and have explained why 1 feel it an honour to second the resolution which was proposed by the hon. member for Kamouraska. Will you let me say in conclusion that I would hope to see this . vexed question settled. Our population is made up of several races true to the institutions of this land and of our great Empire. My trust is that in this moment of great crisis Ontario will send out the message that the word "liberty" is emblazoned upon its shield. My trust is that

Ontario, living up to the principles of its statesmen of the past, will prove that the same unity of intent and purpose exists at home as that which has guided and is guiding the courage, the valour, .and the * heroism of Canadian sons upon the bloodstained battlefields of Flanders. The Empire's dominions are out to uphold nationalization and constitutional' principles. Our sons have crossed the seas ito fight for the oppressed, consecrating with their blood the principles so dear to us, the protection of the .smaller nations, the rights and privileges of Belgium and of Servia, the solidarity of the Empire, the reign of justice and freedom. Such are also the underlying principles of this resolution submitted in the most respectful manner in favour of a race that has no superior in generosity, in liberality, in advancement and in education.

Mr. Speaker, I desire in the first place to assure my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Ernest Lapointe) that there was not the slightest intention on my part to attempt to administer to him any castigation. His speech was couched in very moderate and courteous terms'. His reference to the attachment of French Canadians to their language was touching, and his allusion to the union of our Empire with the French Republic in this war was eloquent. In all he said in both these references I heartily concur. It did not seem to me, however, that any considerable portion of his speech was. especially relevant to the resolution he has introduced. But in so far as it was relevant, it would have been an appropriate speech to address to the proper forum- that is, the Legislature of Ontario.
This motion is addressed to Parliament rather than to the Government; it does not call for any governmental action. Nevertheless, I conceive it my duty, holding the position of leader of the Government, to make my attitude clear in regard to the motion. Notwithstanding what has been urged by my hon. friend from Kamouraska and by my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin), I still adhere to the opinion which I ventured to express yesterday that this motion cannot result in any good and that it may result in much harm. Therefore, as far as I am concerned, I cannot see my way for one moment to support it.
One would have .supposed that there

would have been some effort on the part of the hon. gentleman who proposed the motion to examine the legislation and the regulations which he has called in question by the terms of this motion, and as to which he desires this House to admonish the (Legislature of Ontario and that he would have endeavoured to show in what respect those regulations and the legislation upon which they are founded result in any unfairness or injustice to the French Canadian population of the province of Ontario. Indeed, the fact that my hon. friend has made so little attempt in that regard seems to me a very good reason why this motion should not be accepted by the House if there were no other, and more conclusive, reasons to that effect.
How many hon. members in the House would be prepared to pass an examination upon the effect of the legislation and the regulations of the province in regard to the subject under discussion? Yet, without any inquiry proposed-and the very idea of an inquiry suggests1 the unfortunate character of the proposed resolution-without any inquiry, with only the discussion that can take place in one debate, and without hon. members having before them for their consideration the legislation and the regulations in question, we are asked by this resolution to convey an admonition, to tender advice, to the Legislature of Ontario upon a subject that has been debated and considered most thoroughly and exhaustively in that legislature on many occasions. If we really propose to give advice to the Legislature of Ontario, if a resolution for that purpose could properly be introduced in this iParliament, would it not be reason aJble in the first instance to refer the matter to a committee of this House for the purpose of inquiry and report? Every hon. gentleman realizes that if a proposal for any such inquiry were made, this House would he embarking on a most dangerous and unfortunate course in entertaining it. Yet, without that inquiry, without even an attempt at perusal o>f the legislation and the regulations in question, we are invited to inform the Legislature of Ontario that the policy they have announced and put' into effect, under the legislation which they have passed and under the regulations which they have enacted, is not in accord with right and justice and that they should take our advice upon the question and amend their ways in that respect. It seems to me that the proposition needs only to be
stated to this House in order to make us realize how impossible of acceptance is the proposal which my hon. friend from Kam-ouraska and my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin) have submitted for the approval of the House.
Reference was made by my hon. friend from Wright to an alleged interference with, and reference was made by my hon. friend from Kamouraska to an alleged attempt to proscribe, the French language in Ontario. I do not propose to examine that question. It is not the duty, as I understand it, of a member of this House to examine and pass upon legislation and regulations which are entirely within the control and jurisdiction of the Provincial Legislature and the Provincial Government; but I mav remark in passing that I have given some consideration to this subject. I have tried to understand it, conceiving it to be my duty, that -I should make myself acquainted with a matter which has aroused a certain feeling, a certain controversy, not only in the province of Quebec but in other parts of this country. I have been told by those who are in a position to be informed on the subject that the province of Ontario maintains a number of schools for the training of bilingual teachers; that it provides travelling expenses for teachers whose mother tongue is French in order that they may receive necessary training and acquire proficiency in both languages; that it provides their board and their expenses while receiving this training; that it provides tuition free; and that finally a special grant is made to bilingual schools in order that teachers so trained may be employed in such schools. It does not appear to me that a policy which produces such results can be fairly described as intended to proscribe the French language in Ontario.
As far as the general nature of the regulations is concerned, I do not feel called upon to discuss them, but I will invite the attention of the House to certain considerations which in my judgment make it undesirable that we should accept the motion of my hon. friend from Kamouraska. I thoroughly understand and entirely appreciate the natural attachment of the people of French origin in this country to their own language. I realize also that this attachment was taken into consideration by the Fathers of Confederation and as a result section 133 of the British North America

Act was incorporated in our Constitutional Act, and it is in these terms:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the Houses of Parliament of Canada and of the Houses of the Legislature of Quebec; and both those languages shall be used in the respective Records and Journals of those Houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this Act, and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
The Acts of the Parliament of Canada and of the Legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
That is the only provision of the Constitutional Act so far as language is concerned; and it is imy understanding that it gives the French and English languages the status of official languages in federal affairs and in the public affairs of the province of Quebec, that is to say, in the federal parliament, in the federal courts, in the Quebec legislature and- in the Quebec courts.
Subject to that provision, I would understand, so far as my knowledge extends, that the provinces of Canada have plenary power to deal with the question of language within their territorial limits. That is my comprehension of the provisions of the constitution of Canada as it is embodied in the Constitutional Act.
I realize that in Federal affairs both these languages occupy an official status, and when I entered public life in this country, and more especially when I became the leader of one of its great political parties, I conceived it my duty, so far as the demands upon my time and energy would permit, to improve my knowledge of the French language and my acquaintance with it. It seemed to me no more than my duty that I should do that, in order that I might converse with and write to persons of French origin in their own language, and might address public gatherings of my fellow-citizens of French origin, for a few moments at least, in their mother tongue. And I, for one, would resist with the utmost determination any attempt emanating from any quarter to interfere with the status of the French language as it is fixed in the Constitutional Act of our country. No one of my fellow-citizens of the province of Quebec could be animated with a more intense determination to uphold the rights of the French language in this country, as they are fixed by the Constitutional Act, than I would be if any attempt were made to assail those rights. But I have a great

respect for the Constitution, and I think that until that Constitution is altered in the regular and approved manner, and by approved and constitutional methods, it is our duty to respect and observe it; and it is for this reason that I consider the motion which my ihon. friend has proposed to the House to-day as not in the best interests of this country. I will go further, and say that in my judgment it is absolutely opposed to the best interests of the province of Quebec itself.
Section 91 of the British North America Act sets forth the powers and authorities which are possessed and shall he exercised by the Parliament of Canada. Section 92 of the same Act sets forth the powers and authorities which are possessed and may be exercised by the several provinces of Canada. Section 93 of the British North America Act contains certain provisions with regard to educational matters which confide the subject of education generally to the provinces, with certain limitations in respect of rights which were possessed at the time of the entrance of the several provinces into Confederation, and in respect also of rights subsequently acquired. My hon. friend the member for Kamouraska says that this motion does not call for the disallowance of any Ontario Act. He is absolutely correct in that. He would have been more within his constitutional rights if he had come forward with a motion in that regard, because that question was constitutionally before the Government of Canada and had to be dealt with; and for the reason that it was before the Government of Canada, the Parliament of Canada would have had a much better right to discuss that subject for the guidance and information of the Government, than to discuss and consider the question which is now proposed.
Let me point out for one moment the language of a great Liberal of bygone days with regard to that particular provision. I am alluding to the speech of the Hon. Edward Blake in the House of Commons on the 29th of April, 1890. He was not then leader of the Liberal party, but he had held that position, and he occupied a great' place in the ranks of the party at the time he uttered these words (Hansard, p. 4086):
I regard it as settled, for myself at any rate, first of all, that, as a question of policy, there shall be no disallowance of educational legislation, for the mere reason, that, in the opinion of this Parliament, some other or different policy than that which the province has thought

fit to adopt would be a better policy. I hold it to be settled, in the second place, that no address to the Crown shall be passed by this Parliament asking for a change of the constitutional Act as effecting any province at any rate against the will of that province, in this particular.
First, that Parliament, because it disapproved of provincial legislation in educational matters, should not seek to have that legislation disallowed merely for the reason that Parliament might think a better policy could be adopted; and, secondly, that without the consent of any province of Canada no change should be made in the Constitutional Act so far as such change might affect that province. No appeal as before Parliament at the present time, from the minority either in Ontario or in Manitoba; no question of disallowance is raised by the resolution; and therefore I venture to submit to the House with a great deal of confidence that there is no constitutional sanction under which we can be called upon to advise, or admonish or rebuke the Legislature of Ontario upon a subject entirely within the jurisdiction of that province.
What was the record in 1896, when the subject was constitutionally before Parliament? The result of the attempt then made to carry out the provisions of section 93 was not a very encouraging one, and I think with that opinion my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, who opposed inters ference at that time, will entirely agree. Let us remember that, subject to the provisions of section 93 and subject to the provisions for disallowance of provincial legislation, the provinces of Canada are as sovereign and supreme in their sphere as is the Parliament of Canada in its own sphere. That principle has been established and laid down by the courts. No man who has given the subject any 'consideration can gainsay what I have just now affirmed. If I desire to give an authority which I think will appeal to the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, I might quote his own language. In 1896, when he moved the six months' hoist to the Remedial Bill, so-called, he said:
The Imperial Parliament has the power of disallowance, of supervision over the Acts of these colonial legislative bodies. This may be easily understood because colonies are dependencies. But the relations between the Dominion and the provinces are not the same.
Between these there is no superiority and no inferiority, all are equal, with this exception, that the Dominion Parliament is Invested with larger powers, that is, powers of a more extended and more important character than the
local legislature. Indeed, It must be accepted and accepted as a truism that under popular government the majority must rule.
A little further on (he said:
The remedy of the minority under a free gov. ernment is to agitate and endeavour to bring over a majority to their way of thinking. This is the rule under free government.
He .spoke of a supposed power of the Imperial Parliament to supervise the Acts of Colonial Legislative bodies, and then he went on to declare that, even if that power were possessed by the Imperial Parliament, no such power exists in the Parliament of Canada to supervise the legis'-lation enacted by the Provincial Legislatures. If the principle embodied in this resolution is not an attempt to supervise the legislation of the province of Ontario, I do not know how to characterize it. We are called upon to consider legislation which is not before us, to take into account regulations with which we are not familiar, and then we are invited to give to the Legislature of the province of Ontario an admonition which cannot fail to be understood 'by that Legislature as a reflection upon the policy which it has approved and upon the legislation which it has enacted. That was not my right hon. friend's view in 1896, because when the question was then constitutionally before the Parliament of Canada, it was his view that there should be no interference. When the question is not constitutionally before the Parliament of Canada, why then should there be interference? He denounced the attempt of Sir Charles Tup-per's Government to proceed with the Remedial Bill because, he said, there had not been sufficient inquiry. How does he reconcile that with his proposal to-day to consider and to cast reflection upon legislation of the province of Ontario without any .inquiry at all?
He put forth views in even more distinct terms in the same debate, in a quotation which I shall now give:
For, Sir, experience has taught us that this remedy of interference with local legislation has never been applied and probably never can be applied without friction, disturbance and discontent; that you cannot apply that remedy without causing as much dissatisfaction as satisfaction.
If we are to accept my right hon. friend's words in the spirit in which they were uttered, and to give them all the effect which he intended, that quotation alone ought to be regarded by the House as a just reason for rejecting the motion of my hon. friend from Kamouraska.

The resolution then proceeds, as I have said, to advise and admonish the Legislature of Ontario. Let me take an illustration. I understand that certain legislation was passed at the last session of the Legislature of Quebec, to which some portion of the people of Ontario take exception.
Would my hon. friend say that if a resolution were introduced into this House commenting upon that legislation and recommending to the Legislature of Quebec that it should not continue or persevere in such a policy, we should adopt it? So far as I am concerned, if any such resolution were introduced into this Parliament for the purpose of conveying admonition or rebuke to the

The resolution of my hon. friend in its concluding words is of a significance which I do not fully comprehend.
