The change seems to give a somewhat different purport to the resolution. As it stood at first, before the change was made, it read in this way:
That this House especially at this time of universal sacrifice and anxiety, when all energies should be concentrated on the winning of the war, would, while fully recognizing the principle of provincial rights and the necessity of every child being given a thorough English education, respectfully suggest to the Legislative Assembly the wisdom of making it clear that the privilege of the children of French parentage of being taught in their mother tongue is not interfered with.	.
The purport of the resolution as it stood at first was a suggestion that the Legislature of Ontario should make it clear that the privilege of being taught in French is not interefered with; that is to say, they shornd make the effect of their existing policy perfectly plain. But as altered, the suggestion is that the privilege of being taught in French shall not be interfered with. Although the words are perfectly courteous; although the language is respectful, that is a suggestion-more than that, a dictation-to the province of Ontario as to what its future policy in that regard should be. I repeat that no good purpose can be served, in respect of matters entirely within provincial jurisdiction, by any attempt of this Parliament to examine, to consider, to advise or to dictate to any province.
My right hon. friend, speaking on this subject yesterday, in the course of the brief discussion that we had in the House, said:
Let us discuss it; let us hear both sides of it; and then. Sir, I believe that from this dis-

cussion we shall rise wiser and better men, knowing better what our position is, knowing better what the rights of the minority are; and I venture to say that when the question has been settled, as it ought to be settled, the minority will accept the situation whatever it may be.
I am not quite clear as to what my right hon. friend intended by that suggestion. If he means the legal rights as established by the constitution, then I would respectfully suggest to him that it is not the function of this Parliament to settle or determine them. That is the function of the constituted courts of this country which have been established for that purpose. They alone can deal with such questions, subject to a final appeal to His Majesty in the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. But my right hon. friend may mean something more than that. He may mean that we are to settle in this Parliament the question as to whether there should' be some amendment to the British North America Act by which the rights of the provinces in respect of language or otherwise should be cut down and the constitution amended in that respect.
I point to the opinion of the Hon. Edward Blake, which I read a moment ago, and which, in a few words, is this, that no change of the constitutional Act as affecting any province can be made against the will of that province. Surely it is not [DOT]suggested by my right hon. friend that the Parliament of Canada, without any consultation with the provinces, against the consent of the provinces, can pass or ought to pass an address to His Majeety for the purpose of so amending the British North America Act that the rights of the provinces of Canada shall be cut down and limited. Is there any hon. gentleman in this House who will uphold a proposal of that kind? I venture to think that the view which the Hon. Edward Blake in 1890 announced is not only in the interests of this Dominion as a whole, not only in the interests of all the provinces, but eminently in the interests of the province of Quebec. It is, I repeat, eminently in the interests of the province of Quebec itself. If it were possible for this Parliament, without the consent of the provinces affected, to pass a resolution upon which should be founded an amendment to the British North America Act cutting down provincial rights, no province in Canada would be in a more unfortunate situation than Quebec. We know that for this very reason, because Quebec desired to maintain

control of her own provincial affairs, Quebec was not willing to accept the legislative union which Sir John A. Macdonald desired. As a result we have a Federal constitution and not a legislative union. If my right hon. friend does not suggest that by the language which he used yesterday, I should like to know what he does suggest, and perhaps he will inform us when he comes to address the House. Mt. Speaker, I rise in support of the motion of my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Ernest Lapointe). I approach the subject, however, in a very different spirit from the spirit which has been indicated by the observations of the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government. I rise for the purpose of speaking with as much moderation As I can, and to appeal, not to passion or prejudice, but to the sober reasoning and judgment of my fellow countrymen of all origins. I discard at once all reference to constitutional arguments. I do not here and now bring within the purview of this discussion the British North America Act. I do not here and now invoke the cold letter of any positive law. Still less do I question the paramount power of the Legislature of Ontario to finally pass judgment upon this question and record the final verdict of its people. I rise, sir, not for the purpose of giving aavice or admonition to the province of Ontario. I rise to plead before the people of Ontario, in behalf of His Majesty's subjects of French origin in that province, who complain that, by reason of a statute passed by the province, they have been deprived of rights, in matters of education, which they have enjoyed, themselves and their forefathers before them, ever since Canada became a possession of the British Crown.
And if I take t'hie course, I am impelled to do it by reasons which, in my judgment, are stronger than any that are contained within the four corners of the statute complained of. If there be those-and, if I am right, my right hon. friend is one of them -who tell me that I have no right to come

before this Parliament to plead the cause which I am now pleading, that I am debarred from pleading it, and that the only forum before which it can be pleaded is the Legislature of Ontario, I tell my right hon. friend, and his friends beside him, that it was only four or five weeks ago that I was appealed to by an important organ of an important section of the province of Ontario-I mean the Orange Sentinel-under the signature of its editor, Mr. Hocken, to interfere in this matter, to give my views to my fellow countrymen and endeavour to put an end to the unfortunate agitation that is now going on. The very fact that I was thus appealed to shows that in the language of its editor, at all events, if I understand the English language aright, the question is not confined to the province of Ontario, but has gradually extended beyond its boundaries. I thank Providence that I have lived long enough to see the old enmity of France and England at last at an end and replaced by feelings of cordial and mutual respect and good will towards one another. I thank Providence that I have seen this alliance which gives evidence of being the dawn of eternal friendship between those two nations, an alliance so lofty in purpose that already it is looked upon as one that must last forever-a war between England and France to-day wmuld be just as criminal as a civil war in either of those nations; an alliance

which has received its last consecration in the resolution adopted by the inter-parliamentary committee of France and England, suggesting to 'both nations that the study of their language should be made compulsory in all the schools of Great Britain and France.
Well, Sir, uhfortunately it has not always been so. England and France, as we know only too well, have filled the modern era with the history of their wars. They have fought in 'Europe, and they not onlly fought in Europe, but carried their quarrels and their wars to the virgin wilderness of this vast continent. The virgin wilderness of this continent resounded with the clash of their arms, and the war between them only ended with the final defeat of France. That defeat,	however, was not on
the plains of Abraham, which witnessed the victory of Wolfe over Montcalm; for, immediately after the defeat, the French army was rallied by the Chevalier do (Levis, who for one year maintained the unequal contest, until, in the month of (September, 1760, when the French army found itself between the army of General Murray and the approaching army of General Amherst, he surrendered, And that was the finish forever of the dream of a French Empire on the banks of the St. Lawrence. But there were 60,000 colonists who were then to become British subjects, and whose fate was a cause of anxiety to General de Levis. In the articles of surrender, he asked the victorious general that these 60,000 colonists should be granted their civil rights and the freedom of their religion. The articles were at once conceded 'by the generous victor, and when he had doubts he wrote: " they became subjects of the King ", implying that in that fact there was ample protection.
I am a descendant of those colonists, and [DOT] I am bound to say, what I have repeated many times but never with more pleasure than on the present occasion, that my fellow countrymen under the British Crown have found ample justice and liberty. But, at the same time, no one can deny that there have been jarrings and quarrels between the different elements. We should not be surprised at that, because we have the testimony of history that race quarrels are very persistent and will continue sometimes long alfter the cause which brought them about has disappeared. However, with all the jarrings and ail the quarrels that, we have had, there is one thing upon
which, for more than 150 years, there never was any friction whatever, and that is the subject of education. From the day that Canada became an English possession, and when the French settlements, extended all along the St. Lawrence from Gaspe up to the Detroit river, from that day in 1760 down to about 1885, there never was the slightest friction upon the matter of education.
The French colonists were allowed, in Ontario as everywhere else, to have their schools and to teach their language to their children. (So it was so long as Canada remained a Crown colony; so it was after the two provinces of Upper and Lower Canada had been separated and given an embryo constitutional Government; so it was after Canada had been re- ' united and given responsible Government; and so it was after Confederation and down to the year 1885, when the rights of the French people with regard to education were first challenged. That was in the province of Ontario. That was under the Government of Sir Oliver Mowat, and the old veteran, to his credit be it ever said, rose up to the highest possible notch of magnanimity in standing for the rights of the French minority. He established, or rather he reorganized, the bilingual schools, and these schools gave satisfaction to the minority for many years and to th,e majority as well, until at last, six or seven years ago, it was complained that they had 'become inefficient. As to that I have no opinion to express. I grant that the schools may have become inefficient; but, if the schools had become inefficient 't wks not because the system was defective, but it was because the system was not properly enforced; and in my judgment the efficient remedy would have been to have had this system of schools carried out as it was conceived. But, instead of that," the Board of Education first, and the 'Legislature of Ontario afterwards, passed regulations which it is claimed by the French minority in Ontario interfered seriously with their efficiency and made them almost nugatory and barren' of results.	The French people have accepted the situation everywhere except in the city of Ottawa. They have accepted these regulations but under protest.	They have appealed to^ the
courts against them, and the appeal is still pending before the courts. They have been unsuccessful before the courts of the province, but they have carried their rights to the

foot of the Throne, to the Privy Council, and there the matter rests 'at the present time.
In addition, they have asked for disallowance of this legislation. The Government have refused the petition for disallowance, and as to that I have no fault to find. I have no quarrel, with the Government. I do not know that they could have taken any other course. The remedy by disallowance is very illusory. It is not a positive remedy; it is a negative remedy; the Government can annul a law, hut it cannot do any more than that. Our experience for many years has been that disallowance- and I have no word to change in what was quoted of some of my former utterances a moment ago by my right hon. friend-has not given satisfaction. Instead of giving satisfaction, it has been the cause of many of the agitations which we have had in this country. If the statute were disallowed what would be the result? The result would be that at the ensuing session the same law would be passed by the same legislature. I have no doubt whatever that many of the signers of the petition, and there were thousands of them, thought that by signing this petition and having the law disallowed, that would be the end of it, and that the Legislature of Ontario could thereby have its power curtailed and could not re-enact such a law. But that is a mistake; there is no such thing. If the law had been disallowed, there was nothing to prevent it from being re-enacted, and again re-enacted it would certainly have been.
But, while I do not blame the Government of Canada for having refused to disallow the law of Ontario, I am sorry that I have to express my regret that the Government did not think it advisable, as they had the power to do, to call the attention of the Legislature and Government of Ontario to the complaints of the minority and ask them to give them favourable consideration. My right hon. friend knows-everybody knows-that time and again, under Liberal Administrations and under Conservative Administrations as well, the Government, while refusing to disallow a law, would call the attention of the Government of the province to the fact that there were complaints against that legislation, and suggest to them that it would be wise to give heed to them and try to meet those complaints. Sometimes these remonstrances have been accepted, sometimes they have not been accepted; but I claim that it would have ESir Wilfrid Laurier.]
been a wise action on the part of the Government of the day to have made at least to the (government of Ontario some representation in that behalf.
Now, the matter rests. The only remedy is the remedy in the courts. For my part, I look upon the remedy in the courts under the present circumstances as a very illusory one. There has been, and there is at the present time, an agitation going on that has involved a great deal of bitterness and antagonism which, no judicial decision can allay. We have had the experience of the last fifty years that when rights are vehemently asserted on the one hand and haughtily denied on the other, a judicial decision, while it may enforce, on one side or the other a grudging assent, will not promote harmony, will not create good-will-and harmony and good-will are the considerations which are to be sought first, last, and all the time.
And now, Sir, if my right hon. friend wants to know why I support this motion, as I do, it is not that we wish to force upon the people of Ontario our way of thinking, or compel them to a course they do not want; we have no right to do that. But it is to ask them to consider the situation in 'the light of the present agitation, and to investigate the claims which, in their opinion, may or may not be well founded but for which, at all events, I would ask respectful consideration. My right hon. friend asked me what I meant yesterday when I said I hoped the matter would be discussed here. I want to have the matter discussed here so that on all sides we may frankly approach the subject from the basis of our common Canadian nationality, and, if possible, find a meeting ground where we shall be able to say to the minority: "You shall not go further than that," and to the majority, " You should grant what is reasonable; you should, at all events, make some concession." I ask no more than that. I read a few days ago in a paper of this city the following statement, to which I ask the consideration of the House:
The position of English-speaking Ontario is this-and let any Canadian who has any sense of national responsibility, be he French-speaking or English-speaking, try to understand it and use his influence accordingly before the racial fanatics of this city get their compatriots into fatal trouble. Ontario proposes to remain an English-speaking province in so far as the wishes of her present English-speaking people can prevail constitutionally.

I could quote hundreds of articles of the same nature, in which it is asserted, and again asserted, that Ontario is an Englishspeaking province, and will remain an English-speaking province. Who asks for anything else? There is an impression, I know, among some of my fellow countrymen whom I see on the other side of the House that the French Canadian has some sinister motive behind this agitation, that in some way he wants to get control of the province of Ontario. Sir, the idea would be ridiculous if it were not so serious as it is. But we know there are extremists everywhere; there are extremists who are to-day using language which I reprove as much as does any man of English origin. I am not asking anything at the present time for my Frenchspeaking countrymen of the province of Ontario, except the privilege of having their children taught in the French language untrammelled-a privilege they . have had for at least one hundred and fifty years. Will any one tell me that if the French Canadians of the province of Ontario are allowed to have their children taught in a language which is so dear to them-the French language at that, one of the noblest on earth-that Ontario will be less British than it is to-day? Will any one tell me that, if the people of Wales are deprived of the schools they have a right to, and of the use of their language in those schools in order that their children may acquire it, Wales will be less British than it is at the present moment or has been ever since it was joined to the British Crown? These are some considerations which I wish to place before my fellow-countrymen. Yesterday, when I stated upon the floor of the House that I wanted to have this question discussed, it was in the hope that discussion of it would make us wiser and better men, and that we should understand exactly where we were. There never is harm to be apprehended from a free discussion, and I hoped for a great deal of good. I meant nothing more than that.
Before I go further let me again refer to the open letter which the Orange Sentinel addresssed to me, urging me to interfere in this matte'r. Addressing itself to me it says:
Settle the bilingual controversy by convincing your people that they have no rights in Ontario, and we may look for a better recruiting record in Quebec.
Sir, I am not prepared to say that my fellow-countrymen of French origin have
no rights in Ontario; but I am prepared to say this, and I want my words to. be heard throughout* the length and breadth of this land: whether my fellow-countrymen have rights or no rights in Ontario, whether those rights are granted or denied, these considerations are no bar to the duty which the French-Canadians owe to themselves and to the honour of their race to come forward in their fullest numbers and take part in the great struggle that is going on to-day in the land of their ancestors for the cause of freedom, and of the civilization of mankind.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock, I was speaking of the rights of the French minority in the province of Ontario. -1 stated that I was not prepared to say that the minority had no rights; on the contrary, I would be prepared to argue that under section 93 of the British North America Act the minority has rights which can be enforced in the courts of law. But I repeat what I said previously in the debate, that I do not approach this question upon the cold letter of the positive law. My aim and purpose in approving of the resolution of my hon. friend from Kamouraska is rather to appeal to the sense of justice of the province of Ontario-justice between man and man, justice not according to the letter of the statute, but justice according to the conscience of every living man, no matter what his nationality may be.
I will now put forward the view which I intend to present to the House upon this aspect of the question. I referred this afternoon to the capitulation of Levis to the forces of 'General Amherst in the year 1760. In those Articles of Capitulation no mention is made of language; neither is any mention made of language in the Treaty of Baris which confirmed the terms of the capitulation of Montreal. The only things which are referred to in the Articles of Capitulation and in the Treaty of Paris, are religious freedom and civil rights. There are, however, jurists of eminence who hold it as a canon of the law of nations that civil rights carry with them as a corollary the rights of language. I will not say that the opinion is unanimous, but it is held by authorities of the most eminent reputation. But

canons of the law of nations have no sanction. They are binding on conscience; they are binding on honour; but they have no other sanction. Nations can ignore them or nations can respect them. Nations there are which ignore them; nations there are which respect them. Germany is one of the nations which ignores the canons of the law of nations. She has given in the present war example after example of that contemptuous unconcern, not only in this war, but even in times of peace, and in .the events which followed war. The last instance that we have had of the policy followed by Germany is the case of Alsace-Lorraine after the Franco-Prussian war. By the treaty of Frankfort the provinces of Alsace and Lorraine were detached from France and annexed to Germany. She ignored all the canons of the law of nations and planted her brutal heel upon those two provinces, - ignoring the rights and privileges which, under another regime, the population of those provinces would have had a right to expect. She subjected the French language to many cruel restrictions and indignities. But England, I am proud to say, has always respected the canons of the law of nations. Wherever England has planted her colours by conquest, by treaty, or in any other manner, she has always respected the laws, the language and the religion of her new subjects. The last instance of that, is South Africa. She acted in that manner in Canada; she did it in India; she did it in Mauritius; she did it in Malta; she did it in the West Indies. Wherever she planted her flag the law of nations was observed, and the language of her new subjects was so welj respected that no one would have suspected that there had been a change of allegiance. How many years have elapsed since we were at war with South Africa? Hardly fourteen years. But I am proud, as a British subject, to say that to-day the Dutchman of South Africa i-s just as free to speak his language and to have his children educated in his language as he was before the South African war. All that I have to ask my fellow-Canadians of the province of Ontario is; which example are we going to follow? Which is the best polity for Canada? Is it the German polity? No one will say that. Well, then, will it not be the British polity, which for two centuries or more has been invariably followed in every part of the globe? I could follow the whole circle of the earth and everywhere I would find the same story re-
peated by every British subject, no matter what his origin, whether he is in Malta, where he speaks the Italian language, or in St. Lucia, in the West Indies, where he speaks the French language, or in South Africa, where he speaks the Dutch language, nay, even whether in India, where he speaks languages almost without number. The same story is repeated everywhere, and what I have to propose to my fellow countrymen in the province of Ontario is that we should follow the example of England in the polity she has adopted in all parts of the world. All I ask is that in the province of Ontario, and also in the province of Manitoba, our children should be allowed to be taught in the language of our ancestors:	in Ontario, because the
language was preserved by the Crown itself; in Manitoba, because, when that province was created, the French language was introduced therein by the deliberate will and action of this Parliament.
Speaking of Manitoba, I was more sorry than surprised at the language of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, as his statements in regard to that province added neither strength nor dignity to his argument. He endeavoured to compare my conduct of to-day with my conduct of 1896. Is there any parity or disparity between my conduct of to-day and my conduct of 1896? What was the situation in 1896? Phis Canadian Parliament undertook to pass a law of education for the province of Manitoba over the heads of the Legislature of Manitoba. Did I and my friends undertake to do anything of this kind? Did we attempt to force upon the people by the will of this Parliament a law which would be repugnant to the majority of Manitoba? The law which was introduced by the Government of 1896 was obnoxious to the great majority of the people of Manitoba. Sir, is it not a fact that the Legislature of Manitoba, having behind it almost the whole of the people of the province, had put an end to a system of education which they found obnoxious to them? Is it not also a fact that the Canadian ^Government of that day undertook to put a' law upon the statute-book, by the power of the House of Commons and the Senate of Canada, which a large majority of the people of Manitoba resented? Well, Sir, I would not submit to that; I fought that proposed legislation. Is that all that I did? No, I did something else. I did then the very thing that I am doing to-day. I appealed to the

Government of Manitoba, to the legislature and to the people of that province, saying: "Here is a grievance. I do not care whether it is debated or not; I nsk you to be generous to the majority and to correct the evil which you have created". I am glad to say that my appeal was heeded. The Legislature of Manitoba, in response to my appeal, undertook to amend the Act which was agreeable to the majority but obnoxious to the minority, so as to remedy to a considerable extent the grievance of the minority.
My right hon. friend alluded to-day to the fact that that law has just been repealed. Under the remedy which was enacted in the session of 1897 by the Legislature of Manitoba, the minority were allowed to have religious teaching in their schools and the privileges of a French education. As was stated this afternoon by the Prime Minister, the Legislature of Manitoba has repealed the concession which it made in 1897 so far as the French language is concerned. That is true-only too true.
The right hon. Prime Minister reproached us because the hon. member for Kamouraska did not include an appeal to Manitoba in the resolution of this day. I ask if he was very sincere in his regrets? I thought his regrets were more like crocodile's tears than anything else. I understood what was at the bottom of his speech, I had only to look at the face of my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Casgrain) when the Prime Minister uttered those words. I saw an expression of glee on the face of the Postmaster General; he thought it would be a good argument in the province of Quebec. Let me say to my hon. friend the Postmaster General that I do not speak especially for the province of Quebec; I speak for the people of Canada as a whole. This language I shall hold in every part of Canada, whether it be Quebec, Ontario or any other province. In this resolution we did not include the grievance of the minority of the people of Manitoba; the remedy for that will be sought in another way. I will give my hon. friend another reason. So far as I am concerned, if I have advice to give to my fellow-countrymen of French origin I will tell them not to be has'ty, not to be premature, to take their time, to consider what course they should follow. We have not yet heard the voice of the people of Manitoba at the bar of the House of Commons or at the door of the legislature of that province. There is time enough for all this; the situation will be canvassed at the proper time. But, Sir, I resent that in a matter of so great moment an attempt should be made to mix up situations which ought not to be mixed up. I resent any attempt to look at this question from any standpoint except the broad basis of what is reasonable, right, just and fair.
I now come back to the province of Ontario. I have stated that I want to appeal to the sense of justice and fair play of the people of Ontario and to their appreciation of British institutions-mo more. Even if I am in the wrong-and 1 hope I am not-I am sure that a frank understanding between the majority and the minority in the province of Ontario, between the two great elements which compose the Canadian people, may force a solution of this troublesome question. Every man in the province of Ontario, every man in this room who comes from the province of Ontario, whether he sits on that side or on this side, is determined that every child in the province of Ontario shall receive an English education. To that, Sir, I give my fullest assent. I want every child in the province of Ontario to receive the benefit of an English education. Wherever he may go on this continent I want him to be able to speak the language of the great majority of the people on this continent. I want it, I say, not only because it is the law of the province, but because of merely utilitarian considerations. No man on this continent is equipped for the battle of life unless he has an English education. I, if I may be permitted to make a personal allusion to myself, I am of French origin, but every day of my life I have occasion to bless my father for sending me when eleven years of age to an English school. The benefits which I received there I have carried with me up to the present time. I want every child, therefore, to have an English education. Now I come to the point where I want to speak of my fellow-countrymen in the province of Ontario. When I ask that every child of my own race should receive an English education, will you refuse us the privilege of education also in the language of our mothers and our fathers? That is all tha1, I ask to-day; I ask nothing more than that I simply ask you, my fellow-countrymen, British subjects like myself, if, when we say that we must have an English education, you will say:	"You shall have an
English education and nothing else." There are men who say that in the schools of Ontario and Manitoba there should be no

other language than the English language. But, Sir, when I ask that we should have also the benefit of a French education, will you refuse us that benefit?	Is
that an unnatural demand? Is that an obnoxious demand? Will the concession of it do any harm to anybody? And will it be said that in the great province of Ontario there is a disposition to put aTbar on knowledge and to stretch every child in the schools of Ontario upon a Procrustean bed and say that they shall all be measured alike, that no one shall have the privilege of a second education in a second language? I do not believe it; and if we discuss this question with frankness, as between man and man, in my humble opinion, it can yet be settled by an appeal to the people of Ontario. I do not believe that any man will refuse us the benefit of a French education.
Then, in the newspapers, not all, but many of them, of both parties, I have seen the statement made that there is no disposition to curtail the teaching of the French language, and that it is already provided for. Well, sir, I welcome this generous indignation; and, if it be so, as I think I can show, that the teaching of French, which was organized by Sir Oliver Mowat between the years 1880 and 1890, has been very much restricted by Regulation 17, perhaps then we can come to a satisfactory conclusion that will be acceptable to both sides. Sir, I have seen it stated, and it is argued, that Regulation 17 has put no bar to the teaching of the French language. Before reading Regulation 17, may I read Regulation 15? Regulation 15 is as follows:
*
In school sections where the French or German language prevails, the board may, in addition to the courses of study prescribed herein, require instruction to be given in French or German, reading, grammar and composition, to such pupils as are directed by their parents or guardians to study either of these languages.
It is stated that this regulation is still in force, and so it is. It is very plain in its wording. It means this, that in all sections where the German element or the French element prevails, this element can ask the privilege of having its education in either the German or the French language. I repeat that this section is still in force. But it has been modified by Regulation 17, which is in these words:
Section 4. In schools where French has hitherto been a subject of study, the Public or Separate School Board, as the case may be, may provide, under the following conditions, for instruction in French reading, grammar and com-

position, in Forms I to IV, in addition to the subjects prescribed for the Public and Separate Schools.
Mark the words, "in schools where French has hitherto been a subject of study." What is the meaning of the word "hitherto" here, and why has it been introduced? Instead of one condition, which you had previously, you now have two conditions. One condition is that French henceforth is to be taught only in settlements where that language prevails and where it has hitherto been taught. In other words, Regulation 17 has created a restricted atmosphere in which French can be taught. It can continue to be taught, though in modified form, in all the schools where it was taught before June, 1912. But in other schools it cannot be taught. In other words, in no new schools can the French language be introduced. I know that this disposition has been dealt with in other papers. I have seen it denied. But I am told on good authority, and I have reason to believe it is true, that the regulation has been so interpreted as to mean that the French language shall not be taught anywhere except in the schools where it was taught before June, 1912. Will any man tell me that this is a liberal disposition? Will any of my friends sitting in this House tell me that they are satisfied with it? But if I am told-
Will my hon. friend pardon a question? Will he tell us where that interpretation applies?

my hon. friend.

It applies just what the word " hitherto " means, and I ask my hon. friend what the word " hitherto " means. Why is it there?

I will explain when my
time comes.

I will explain now. If the word " hitherto " does not mean anything, strike it out. What will be the remedy I ask? Will my hon. friend agree to that? If it is meaningless why is it there? If it means nothing, why has it been inserted there? If it means what I say, why do you keep it there? Sir, we do not want any of this quibbling between us.
Oh, oh.

I do not want any of this quibbling between us. This word

" hitherto " must mean something or it means nothing. If it means nothing, if it does not mean that the tuition of French is to be restricted to schools where it was taught in 1912, then all I ask is that it be removed, and we shall have no further quarrel. This is my position. I know that it has been so interpreted elsewhere; at all events, I understand so. But if it has been so interpreted elsewhere, by mistake or otherwise, all I ask now is that there shall be no equivocation upon it, and that we shall know exactly where we are.
There is another disposition of Regulation 17 to which I take similarly serious exception. I must say that I have taken a long time to make up my mind as to what was the character of this regulation and what attitude I should take. Looking at those regulations, and giving them the best understanding I can, there is another disposition which I submit to the fairness and justice of my friends, the majority in the province of Ontario. The other thing of which I complain is that the language of tuition between teacher and pupil is made to be the English language for the French children, even in learning English. Between teacher and pupil the English language is made the exclusive language, except under very exceptional circumstances. Here is Regulation 17, paragraph 3:
Subject, in the case of each school, to the direction and approval of the chief inspector, the following modifications shall also he made in the course of study of the public and separate schools.
(1) Where necessary in the case of Frenchspeaking pupils, French may be used as the language of instruction and communication; but such use of French shall not be continued beyond Form 1, excepting that, on the approval of the chief inspector, it may also be used as the language of instruction and communication in the case of pupils beyond Form 1 who are unable to speak and understand the. English language.
What is the meaning of these words, " where necessary "? They did not exist before; they were introduced in June, 1912. Here are a few children between five and six years of age going to school. They have learnt at their mother's knee the French language and no other, and they are told that they must be taught in the English language unless it is found necessary to teach them in the French language. Who is to determine? The chief inspector. Here is a school in the back concessions, and you have to apply to the chief inspector to know whether or not it is necessary that the child should be given the privilege of having an education in the
French language, in his own tongue, and not in English. Why this harsh provision,
I ask? Why this unnecessary and harsh provision? Sir, I am free to say, and I say it without any hesitation, that men are not necessarily or wantonly cruel and offensive. This regulation has been introduced for a purpose, and with an idea. The idea is that the French pupil who comes into school, the young boy who receives his education from the teacher in the English vernacular will make more progress than if he were taught in the French language. I take absolute exception to that view, and I put this as a proposition of schoolteaching under such circumstances that, if you want the child to make progress even in his own language, which is French, or in the English language, the medium of communication between the teacher and the child should be the French language. My proposition is plain. I put it to my hon. friends on the other side, and if I can make it good I hope they will give us the benefit of it. I will not give my own opinion as my authority; I will give authority much higher than my own. In the first place, I will quote upon this very subject the language of a man whose name I had occasion to mention before in this House, and who, though speaking from the grave, is still an authority in the province of Ontario as he was amongst the living; I mean Sir Oliver Mowat. In a speech delivered at Woodstock on December 3, 1889, he spoke upon this very point in these words:
Our opponents pretend that the Government should insist on all instruction being given to the French children in the English language. No such regulation was suggested by the Commissioners-
These were commissioners appointed by Sir Oliver Mowat to investigate the question.
-and none such has been made, because such a regulation would be absurd, and, instead of serving the cause of education, would often prevent education altogether.
This is high authority, I repeat. But I have other authority to submit to the House. The names are not as famous or as well known as the name of Sir Oliver Mowat, but they are the names of experts whose testimony ought to be acceptable, because they are regarded as experts in education in all parts of the British Empire.
In 1911 there was held in London an Imperial conference on education. Mark the words-Imperial conference on education; and a special sitting of the conference was

devoted to bilingualism. The conference on bilingualism took place on the 2nd of May, 1911, under the presidency of the Right Hon. Walter Runciman, then President of the Board of Education, and there were present experts from India, from Canada, from South Africa, from Malta, from Jersey, from the Scottish Education. Department, and from the Board of Education of England and Wales, all countries in which, at that time, and from time immemorial, there has been bilingualism. This subject was canvassed upon every side. I could tell you of the suggestions offered and of the speeches delivered by the delegates from South Africa-Mr. Thomas Muir, Superintendent of Education, Cape of Good Hope, and Mr. Viljoen, a Dutchman, Director of Education in the Orange Free State. It would take too long to go over the whole pamphlet; but I will give the House some of the opinions which were then expressed upon this very topic that we have now under consideration.
In the first place, I will quote the opinion of Dir. MacKay, . Sucerintendient of Education in the province of Nova Scotia:
In Nova Scotia less than 10 per cent are Acadian French. In New Brunswick perhaps less than 20 per cent are Acadian French. For a number of years we endeavoured to give them at least in the common school grades bi-lingual readers with instruction from the beginning in English. It was held by the French that the children could make no progress because they could not understand English when first entering school. In order to settle the difficulty a commission was appointed; and the commission determined, and the Government accepted the determination, that the education of the Frenchspeaking child should commence, and be continued during the first four years in the mother tongue, and French readers were provided for them. While these French readers were used during the first four years the teachers of these schools were expected to acquaint th'emselves with the method of teaching English colloquially, and during these four years the children were required to do as much as possible in English so that after the fourth year instruction could go on in English continuously. That is the way the matter stands at present in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I believe the French are pretty well satisfied with it. The children in this way learn English more easily. They can learn written French more rapidly, and that enables them with very little difficulty, to commence their studies in English thereafter.
Mark the words: children commencing their education in their own tongue can take' up English afterwards more easily. Now, I pause here and aek every man in this House, who has had a bilingual education, if this opinion of Dr. MacKay is not justified to the letter by hie own experience. Where a French child knows his grammar, and has the elements of a 
French education, the complications of the French language are so much more difficult than the complications of the. English language that the task of learning English afterwards is made quite easy. I am sure that every man in this House who hae had' a bilingual education will appreciate and endorse what I say.
But, Sir, the one opinion to which I am anxious to call the attention pf the House is the opinion of Mr. Owen Edwards, Chief Inspector of schools in the Welsh Department of the Board of Education in England, who spoke in this way:
With regard to the teaching of English to Welsh-speaking children, for a certain number of years we tried the method that seems to be condemned unanimously by the Conference to-day. We thought that the best way of teaching English to a Welsh child would be to make language and the atmosphere of the school entirely English, and to use Welsh, if at all, for the purpose of absolutely necessary explanation. I can hut state the result by quoting from a report of a small committee of teachers of great ability and long experience, a report adopted and published by the Anglesey Education Committee. The infant, as he leaves the infant school, is thus described.
" He reads words with which he associates no meaning, and is denied access to the written word which would at once call up ideas and stimulate his intelligence. Thus, when he has attained the age of six or seven, his book tells him nothing; the language he reads he cannot understand, and the language he understands he cannot read."
That was the typical product of our infant schools until a few years ago. As regards the bi-lingual districts, we have to face, in our smaller schools, the difficulty of a double curriculum and a double staff. We avoid both. If about 66 per cent of the children speak English as their home language, we take En glish as the language of the infant school; if about 66 per cent speak Welsh, we take Welsh as the one language. So far, we have had no difficu'ty that has not been easily overcome. Bilingual teachers are easily obtainable.
And he concludes with these words:
The results, so far as we In Wales are concerned, are certainly unmistakable. In the Welsh-speaking district, it is not too much to say that the newer method of teaching by means of the home language has practically doubled the efficiency of the schools. For one thing, it connects the elementary school with the home and with other educational Institutions, especially with two characteristic Welsh institutions : the Sunday School (which is a school for the whole people, not for children only), and the literary meeting. It has also greatly facilitated the learning of English. A child in Standard III, in a school employing the modern method writes English more correctly and reads it more intelligently than a child in Standard V, in a school in which the old method is till used. That is, a Welsh-speaking child .of nine, who has learnt his own language first, will write better English and read English more intel. ligently than a Welsh-speaking child of 11 who has been taught English exclusively from the

first day he entered school. This is""my experience.
Now, I quote to you the opinion of another of these experts in the Welsh language, Mr. A. T. Davies, secretary of the Welsh Department:
So far back as 1S93, the following instruction was issued by the Board of Education to Her Majesty's Inspectors acting in Wales :
" In the case of Wales it is clearly established that in many cases in Welsh-speaking districts the use of Welsh in the school, side by " side with English, will greatly facilitate an intelligent understanding of English. It is desirable that the attention of teachers should be called to this question, and that Her Majesty's Inspectors should encourage the practice of bi-lingual teaching by themselves making use of Welsh in testing children's intelligence. The use of Welsh songs and Welsh poetry in the schools in question will he of considerable service."
Now, I pass to another expert, Mr. Warre Cornish, who represented the Scottish department of the Board of Education. Mr. Warre Cornish expressed his opinions in these words:
The department refrain from laying down the law as to the bi-lingual problem; only they are careful that in the Gaelic-speaking districts there shall be an inspector, generally a Highlander, who thoroughly understands the difficulties of the problem, and who is in very close touch with the teachers, and it is left very much between the two parties; and I can only' say that, so far as I am aware, this method of leaving the problem to settle itself on the spot has worked with very general satisfaction to the parents.
Of course there are enthusiasts for the Gaelic language and extremists who may make their voice heard sometimes, but there has been very little complaint from the parents that that language is not receiving sufficient attention.
Dr. Viljoen:	Is it used as a medium in any
way?
Mr. Warre Cornish : There is no provision for or against the use of Gaelic as a medium.

It is occasionally used as
a medium in some schools, is it not?
Mr. Warre Cornish:	It certainly is used as
a medium.
In the face of these authorities, in the face of these opinions of experts, in the face of the mature reflections of men whose lives have been devoted to teaching in bilingual schools, am I not justified in asking the Legislature of Ontario at all events to give us a rehearing upon this matter? I ask nothing more. I ask to have a rehearing in a matter of such importance to us as-to whether or not the policy which has been adopted by Ontario is right and proper or whether it may be improved.
But when I express this request I know that men will rise up before me
with uplifted hands and say, " Hands off,"-we have heard it to-day from the Prime Minister-. " Hands off; the province of Ontario is an autonomous province, and it will not brook any dictation; the province of Ontario has paramount powers in this matter." The province of Ontario has paramount powers in this matter, and it is for the province of Ontario to say whether or not it will give us that rehearing which I ask for my fellow countrymen of French origin or whether it will refuse it. The province of Ontario has paramount power, but may I not recall to the province of Ontario the words of the great poet:
O, it is excellent
To have a giant's strength, but it is tyrannous
To use it like a giant.
The province of Ontario has paramount power and I would be the last man to question it; I would be the last man to try to interfere with it. I am of the old school of Mowat and Blake, who were the prophets and the originators of the doctrine of provincial rights, and by that doctrine I stand to-day. T say that the province of Ontario will and shall determine that question; but I ask these new converts to the doctrine of provincial rights: Am I interfering with the doctrine of provincial rights when i ask humbly to be allowed to present my petition to the province of Ontario? Is it forbidden in the code of these nev adepts in the doctrine of provincial right! that you shall not even be allowed to stand at the bar of the province of Ontario? and make your plea? I stated at the beginning of my remarks that I did not come here to admonish or advise the province of Ontario; I came here simply to present the petition of a humble subject of His Majesty who happens to have been born of French parents, and who wants to preserve the right which has been preserved to me by the British Crown, a right which has existed as long as the British Crown has had sway in this country.
I know that there is to-day in the province of Ontario a sense of irritation at the position which has been taken by some of my fellow countrymen of French blood in the province of Quebec, who have from the first deprecated the participation of Canada in the present war, and who have exerted their influence to attempt at least to prevent enlistment. Alas, it is true; it is only too true. It is deplorable, and it is to me as unintelligible as it

is deplorable. It is true there are in my province men of French origin who when France is fighting a fight the heroism of which stirs the blood of mankind, remain with their blood cold and tell us: " No, we will not lift a finger to assist England in defending the integrity of France; we want our wrongs to be righted in Ontario." Wrongs or no wrongs there is the field of honour, there is the call of duty. But, Sir, though our cause be just and fair, shall it be impeded because there are men who so far forget the duty which they owe not only to their British allegiance, but to the French blood which flows in their veins. If there are men who have taken that ignoble stand there are many men, also, who have gone to the front, and who are now standing by the side of their British comrades, fighting under the British flag with as much courage as any British soldier.
A pretty small number of them.
Shame.

If anything is to weigh in the balance, is it to be the voice of the shirker, the voice of the slacker, or is it to be the voice of the man who has responded to the call of duty and gone to the front, and who is doing his duty to the Empire, even to the shedding of his blood? Some hon. member says they are few in number. Yes, perhaps not as many as there might have been; I admit that. But, if it is so, where lies the responsibility if it is not w'ith the men who, in 1911, said that under no circumstances should Canada fight for England. I have done my best, at all events. I have given the best of my life for the doctrine that I am now maintaining, not upon this question only, but in the fight for civilization which we aTe now waging on the soil of France. When Gladstone undertook to bind up and heal the wounds of Ireland and to give to that unfortunate country a last measure of liberty and justice, there were extremists among the Irishmen who did all they could to down the policy of the Grand Old Man. They did all they could to continue the old hatred against England, to sow discord, and to fan the passions of that unfortunate, but noble country.. But Gladstone, great man that he was, was not deterred. He went on. Though, like Moses, he did not bring the people to the promised land, he sowed the seed. The seed he 
planted has germinated and brought forth fruit; the cause of Ireland has 9 p.m. grown until it is fully matured, and to-day England is reaping her reward, in the unanimity with which the Irish people stand behind her in this war. Indeed, in spite of all the gold and all the plotting of Germany, which did nothing more than to raise a riot which was at an end after three days at the most, the policy of conciliation inaugurated by Gladstone has been vindicated and the insane plot will not dash from Ireland the cup of fulfilment which was at her lips.
I have lived too long not to know that the distrust that is caused by race quarrels is one of the banes of our life in Canada. If there is this exclusion of the French language which we complain of today in the manner whicK I have stated, is it because there is distrust of the French race? You do not look to the great body of the nation; you look only to certain extremists who have made use of the most detestable language. A journal published in the city of Toronto, edited by a man of great ability, an eminent writer who has given himself the mission of being the foremost advocate of a closer bond of union for the British Empire, has, within the last ten days, inaugurated a new programme, the first article of which is, "One language, and one language only." Under the present circumstances this means that only one language shall be taught in the schools of Ontario. The editor of that paper is not the only man to conceive that the Empire, to be united, must be united not only in aim and in purpose,, but in every detail. Sir, I wonder if this new theory for bringing about unity of the Empire is to be applied in Wales, and the Gaelic language accordingly prohibited in the Welsh schools. Is this theory to be applied in the Highlands of Scotland, or in Malta, or in Egypt, or in South Africa? Sir, if there is one thing which to-day stands to the glory of England-a feat unparalleled in the history of the world-it is that to-day on the battlefield in Flanders there are men who do not speak a word of English, but who for England have come forward to fight and die. If the Britisher, when he went to India, to Malta, to South Africa, or anywhere else, had implanted that new doctrine of "one language and one language only," and had suppressed the language of the people who had just passed under his dominion, do you believe, Sir, you would have seen that great and noble spectacle which has astonished and is still astonishing the

world? No, Sir. It is because British institutions everywhere have carried freedom and respect for minorities that England is as strong as she is to-day.
My right hon. friend, commenting this afternoon upon the resolution which has been introduced by my hon. friend from Kamouraska, and especially upon the words, "That this House, especially at this time of universal sacrifice and anxiety, when all energies should be concentrated on the winning of the war," wondered why this resolution had been introduced in the midst of the war. Can he have any doubt? Does he not see why? I will tell him. It has been introduced in this House for the same reason that a similar motion was introduced at the meeting of the Inter-Parliamentary Committee of the Allies, held in old Westminster Hall. Assembled there to consider means for bringing about the end of the war, the committee declared that it would be in the best interests of unanimity to have the English and the French language taught wherever the banners of France and England floated. It is less than a month since eminent members of the French and English Parliaments met in that old hall to discuss the war and the best methods to be pursued in bringing it to an end, and one of the things which they did suggest was that the French and English languages should be taught where-ever the French or the English ruled. Did they believe that in doing this noble work they were doing anything that would militate against the successful ending of the war? No, Sir, their thought rose higher than that; they believe that in so doing they were fostering the very object which we have in view-and what a lesson it is for us to-day, my fellow-citizens in this House of Commons! Sir, we are engaged in this stupendous war, which is to determine whether or not henceforth might or right is to -rule the world. Alas, it is only too plainly evident that we are still very far from the end. More sacrifices will be needed; more mothers will have to mourn over their lost sons, and more horrors will be piled up on the soil of brave, desolate France and on the soil of unfortunate Belgium. But already to this black cloud there is visible a silver lining. After nearly three months of fearful battering, the citadel of Verdun, ever proud and defiant, still flies' the tri-colour at its masthead. This failure of the German arms makes it very plain that in this contest Germany cannot win- that might cannot triumph over right.
Already it is plain to any observer that in the trenches will be buried many of the old hatreds and old prejudices, and that from the soil of the battlefields will germinate a new spirit of affection and brotherhood, such as has never before been heard of or known since the angels themselves brought from Heaven the divine message of "Peace on earth, good-will to men." We have an earnest of this new spirit of brotherhood in the resolution adopted by the Interparliamentary Committee of France and England, which, as I said, came to us from Westminster Hall itself, that old and noble building which goes back to the time of the Norman Kings and which has seen the development and evolution of all that is contained in those great principles of freedom, justice, and tolerance. That call which was made in Westminster Hall to all British subjects, to all French citizens, I make bold to make here in Ottawa, not in any spirit of dictation, but in the same spirit which has inspired and -is the true spirit of British institutions, in the hope that it will be heard in Ottawa, heard in Toronto, and heard in Winnipeg.

Mr. Speaker, it shall he my duty to bring the attention of the House back to the real question before us, even if we have to descend from the high flights of eloquence attained by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. I was rather surprised this afternoon when my right hon. friend said that he had received from the Orange Sentinel the inspiration to bring this resolution before the House. That, after having been forty years in public life, for twenty-nine years of which he has been the /leader of the Liberal party he should look to the Orange Sentinal for his inspiration to become not the father, but at least the foster-father of this resolution, is, to say the least, somewhat surprising.
When I was practising at the bar I often watched the judges weighing the different arguments pro and con, and sometimes they were so long in coming to the point and rendering their decision that I was inclined to get impatient. I shall not on this occasion give the House time to get impatient awaiting my views on the questions before us. After the most mature deliberation, after having examined the situation, after having -studied the resolution now before the House, and considered whether or not under the present circumstances it can be of any profit, advantage, or benefit to the minority in Ontario or

Northwest Territories. I shall quote from some of the speeches made at that time by eminent men who have now passed away, to show in what spirit the French language was treated -by them. The hon. member for Kamouraska quoted from the remarks made by the late lamented Sir John lA. Macdonald. Let me cite what the Hon. Edward Blake said upon the occasion to which I have referred:
You may selfishly wish that he had agreed to be suppressed; you may have a profound conviction of the incomparable superiority of your tongue, your laws, your creed; you may earnestly desire for all men the inestimable boons of British birth, of English speech, of Protestant religion. But still, after all, cannot you put yourself in his place? And can you not, must you not, admire the courage, the fidelity, and the determination with which, at great odds, he fought in all fields-in the legislature, before the people, and in even sterner fields than these-for what to him was as dear as what you call your birthright is to you? Fought, aye, and conquered too! Cannot you recognise that his was after all a victory for humanity? And that if, as the case is, it has imposed greater difficulties and more arduous efforts and toils on those who are engaged in making a nation of Canada, it yet, by that very circumstance, gave the chance for more exalted triumphs, gave an opening for the exhibition of still higher and deeper and broader feelings of justice and liberality and tolerance than are permitted to a wholly homogeneous people? Can you not at least see-if that much you cannot see-that he has in fact conquered? Do you seriously hope to prevail to-day in a conflict in which, under infinitely greater disadvantages, he obtained the victory long ago? Surely if it were a conquest in which he was in the wrong, you had the right to struggle still; but his victory after all was for equal rights-rights equal with your own. That is all he asked ; that is all he got. But you say: no; his language must be obliterated; it is inimical to the Constitution that it should continue; you must teach him your tongue; he must forget his own; he must not have what he regards-and, from his point of view, rightly regards-as equal rights with you, the Anglo-Saxon, of whom the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) spoke so proudly this afternoon as destined by fate to swallow him up. Sir, I regard this larger question to which I have referred, and it is the real question we have to consider, as a settled question; and even were my views as to the settlement different from what they are, I would not consent, as a public man, to an attempt to reopen a controversy, long since closed, on grounds which do not give to my eye the least prospect of success, but which ensure ultimate defeat to the assailants, and meanwhile limitless disaster to the state. I say: No; a thousand times no! Whether you differ or agree as to what might have been best for the country, in the situation of the country as it stands, I say: No, a thousand times, no; to the least effort or proposal to reopen that settled controversy ; and I maintain that it is the duty of those who truly regard the progress and the prosperity of Canada, who hope to see it advance in its path towards nationality, to defend the rights of the minorities in this regard, as by law and by convention and by national 
settlement established. I intend for my part to defend them just as warmly as if I were one of themselves; and I should regard myself as dishonoured and disgraced if I were now to yield to the forces which press me to any other course.
And Sir John A. Macdonald, on the same occasion on which he used the words quoted by the hon. member for Kamouraska, said this further:
Why, Mr. Speaker, if there is one act of oppression more than another which would come home to a man's breast, it is that he should be deprived of the consolation of hearing and speaking and reading the language that his mother taught him. It is cruel. It is seething the kid in its mother's milk. The greatest, perhaps, of all the objections to this measure, is that it is a futile measure. It will not succeed. It cannot succeed. As my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Mills) said the other day, and as the hon. member from the West Riding of Durham (Mr. Blake) repeated, in order to carry out an oppressive measure we must have a Russian Government or we must have a Stafford here ; we must put down the language with a strong hand ; we must exclude it from the schools; we must exclude it from, official life; no man in Canada who spoke French must be allowed to take office; the Frenchman must be made a Pariah, and his language must be made a mark of scorn; that is the only way to carry out the principle or the object of my hon. friend the minister for North Simcoe.
What was the outcome of this discussion during which these noble words were delivered? It was this that the question was to be left to the Legislatures of the Nbrth-west Territories, when they had received provincial organization. And all these men who spoke in this way of the French language came to the conclusion that this was a question not for the Federal but for the provincial domain. Why has this regard been paid to the French language, by custom, by Acts, by the speeches of eminent men? The French were the first comers in this country; they were the pioneers; they introduced civilization from the Gulf to the Rockies. They were a valourous race, they fell fighting with their faces to the foe. The British respected them, and after a few years gave them more liberal terms, by the Quebec Act of 1874, than were contained in the Capitulation.
Again, I do not put the question upon the legal ground which is submitted to the courts; I put it upon the historical ground, and I join with my right hon. friend in appealing to the generous sentiments of the people of Ontario. If it is true that these regulations are restrictive or prohibitive of the right of teaching French in Ontario, I appeal to the generous sentiment of my fellow Canadians, I appeal

to their sympathy, and I ask them to right what may be a great wrong towards the minority in the province of Ontario.
Mr. PUGSLEY': That is all that anybody wants.
Carried.

My hon. friend from St. John says: that is all that anybody wants. But will the resolution now before the House attain that? Will this resolution allay the agitation which exists in the province of Quebec and in the province of Ontario? I fear not. I shall not follow my right hon. friend or my hon. friend from Kamouraska in the discussion of Regulations 17 and 15, for it is not my province to be informed upon these questions as I would be if I were a member of the Legislature of Ontario. But, if I do not discuss these questions, it is for another reason, and that reason is that I would not wish that any regulation or law emanating from the Legislature of Ontario should be subject to the censure of the House of Commons. If there is one province in the Dominion whose acts it would not be desirable to discuss in this House; if there is one province in the Dominion who should be careful of her autonomy; if there is one province in the Dominion who should be careful that the provincial sphere is not invaded by the federal, it is the province of Quebec. As my honoured leader said this afternoon, at one time it was rumoured-I do not know whether the rumour has ever been substantiated-that during the conferences on Confederation Sir John Macdonald wanted, not a federation as we have to-day, but a legislative union, and it was the province of Quebec which prevented the adoption of that constitutional system. Now, Sir, I put this question to the House: if we discuss to-day the educational affairs of Ontario; if we discuss to-day the educational laws of Ontario; if we discuss to-day the educational laws of Ontario or the educational regulations of the Ontario and Department of Education, is it not a fact that it would be competent for us to discuss in this House any law or any regulation emanating from the Legislature of Quebec?
Does the hon. gentleman imagine that the province of Quebec would pass such a regulation as has been passed in Ontario, or has he ever heard any complaint from the minority in Quebec?

That is not the point at all. There are certain laws which have been passed by the province of Quebec- and I am not blaming the province of Quebec-which have been distasteful to the province of Ontario, and if, because they were distasteful to the province of Ontario, they were brought before this House and condemned or criticised, certainly I would be the first, and I have no doubt my hon. friend would be among those who would oppose any interference by the Federal House in the provincial sphere.
Let me examine this resolution. It says:
That this House especially at this time of universal sacrifice and anxiety, when all energies should be concentrated on the winning* of the war, would, while fully recognizing the principle of provincial rights and the necessity of every child being given a thorough English, education, respectfully suggest to the Legislative Assembly the wisdom of making it clear that the privilege of the children of French percentage of being taught in their mother tongue be not interfered with.
Sir, tii:is resolution either is not sufficient or it goes too far. What does it suggest? It simply suggests that the laws of the province of Ontario be made clearer. WelJ, now, it seems to me that it is not for us! that we have no mandate in this House, and that we have not sufficient knowledge, to say to the province of Ontario that its laws are not clear enough, that its laws do not clearly say such and such a thing which we would like them to say. My humble opinion is that this resolution is not only absolutely useless, but harmful. It is fraught with great danger to the other provinces, and especially to the province of Quebec.
What would be the result if this resoffi-tion passed the House? Supposing, for instance, the majority of this House passed the resolution in question. What would we do? How would we make the suggestion to the Legislature of Ontario, and bow would it be received by that legislature? That is what we have to ask ourselves. What reception would it get by the Legislature of Ontario and what good would it do? What good would it do? Supposing we passed this resolution and sent it to the Legislature of Ontario, what would happen? Sir, I have only to read some of the extracts from the press of the province of Ontario to show you what reception a suggestion of that kind would get from the province of Ontario, and from the Legislature of Ontario. The Toronto Star was one of the most sympathetic organs of public

opinion in Ontario to the cause of the minority, but it said on the 14th of April:
No row that can be raised at Ottawa, no play that can be made on the rivalry between the two political parties in Canada, will be of any avail whatever in modifying Ontario's position in this matter. In no school in the province will English be excluded. It will be taught by a teacher who knows how to teach English. The inspecting will be done by an inspector competent to see that the teaching is done.	.
That much being assured, the province of Ontario is disposed to be quite reasonable as to details.
Again, on the 27th of April it said:
Those who are seeking Federal interference in the present case may succeed in fomenting strife and increasing difficulty, but they will not help the French-Canadian in Ontario. To any conciliatory suggestion there can, of course, be no objection, but all notion of disallowance, or of any kind of coercive action, must be abandoned. For that reason, we see no advantage in starting any kind of debate in the House of Commons at Ottawa. Such a debate would be misunderstood.
Then, the Toronto Globe, not the Orange Sentinel, but the Globe of the 10th of May, eaid:
Canada is a Confederation. The Federal Parliament seems to forget that fact occasionally, when it gives advice to the provinces.
That is the reception which any suggestion from this Parliament to the province of *Ontario would get. Who are taking part in this agitation and where does the agitation exist? It exists in the province of Quebec, and in the province of Ontario, and I say that by bringing this ^ question up in the Federal House and asking us to pass this resolution, those responsible are sowing discord in this country, which will spread from one end of Canada to the other.
The resolution is insidious. It is skilfully drafted; it is drafted in such a way as to appear harmless to the uninitiated, who do not appreciate the distinction between the federal power and the provincial power, or between the executive power and the judicial power. After all, if the law is not clear, it is is being submitted to the courts for definition. There are two cases now which are on their way to the Privy Council, one in which the constitutionality, the validity and the meaning of Regulation 17 are submitted to the Privy Council, and the other in which the law which applies more particularly to the the city of Ottawa, and which substitutes a commission for trustees, is to be tested. Why should we, when these two cases are before the courts, seek to substitute the interpretation of 
this House for the interpretation which is being sought by the frier ds of the minority in the courts of this country? I say it is a dangerous principle to mix up in this manner the legislative power with the judicial power.
It is said that we have the expressive power. It may be so, but when the powers are defined by our constitution, as clearly as they are with respect to education, this Parliament, when it uses that expressive power in respect to subjects which are allotted to the provincial authorities invades a sphere from vhich it has been expressly excluded in regard to legislation or an expression of an opinion. There was one aspect of the question which could probably have been brought before this House, allusion to which has been made this afternoon, and that is, disallowance of the Act passed by the Legislature of Ontario in 1915, which was asked for by a great many people in the province of Quebec especially, and in the city of Ottawa. That was a proper matter to be brought before this House, as was correctly stated by my ^ hon. friends who have preceded me, and I was glad to hear them say so. The right hon. leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Kamouraska have said that they approved of the action of the Government in not disallowing that Act.# If we were right in not disallowing the Act, how is it that hundreds and thousands of signatures were procured in the province of Quebec and in Ontario asking us to disallow it? Was it for the purpose of keeping up the agitation, and is it by such means that the agitation is being kept up not only in the province of Quebec but in other parts of the Dominion? The fact that we have not been blamed, that no member of this House has dared to rise and condemn the Government for not disallowing the Act of the Ontario Legislature is not only a vindication of the position we have taken, but a condemnation of those who have gone around in the province of Quebec and in the province of Ontario gathering those signatures to a petition, the prayer of which finds no supporters amongst the 221 members of this House.
Questions similar to this have occupied the attention of this House in times gone by. I remember well when the Jesuits' Estates Bill passed by the Legislature of Quebec in 1888 was brought before this House in 1889. That Act was distasteful to a large proportion of the citizens of Ontario; it was distasteful also to a large proportion of the Protestants in the province of Quebec. The matter was brought be-

fore this House, and I am proud to say that under the leadership of the late Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir John Thompson, the principle was laid down that there should be no interference with provincial legislation by the Federal Parliament. The principles upon which Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir John Thompson, and the Conservative party acted in those days in respect to an Act passed by the Legislature of Quebec are the principles upon which this Government stands to-day. In refusing to interfere, to admonish, or to suggest Jo the province of Ontario in relation to a measure which is within its competency, we are only following the precepts laid down in this House by Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir John Thompson, and the other former leaders of the Conservative party. [DOT] I appeal to my hon. friends from the province of Quebec to-day to follow the example of the Conservative party, and especially of the English members of the Conservative party, in 1889, when, notwithstanding the fact that it was a Bill passed by the province of Quebec, a Bill which was distasteful to the great majority of Protestants in this country, the English-speaking Conservatives and the Protestant Conservatives of the House of Commons stood by Sir John A. Macdonald, by Sir John Thompson, and by the province of Quebec, in declaring that they would not interfere with provincial legislation.
I know perfectly well that I am running counter to the feeling of a large majority in my province, but in my sober judgment I think I am right. Let the storm gather, let the clouds burst and the thunder roll; ,the tempest will pass away, and to those who come after me I leave my defence.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to address the House in respect to the resolution now before you,I am well aware that the course I am about to take may be misunderstood. It is always easy to avoid a difficulty of a transient nature, but there are issues of a higher order which compel a man with a sense of duty to face them squarely, come what may. The present resolution, moderate in form, gives expression to a sentiment and embodies a principle which cannot but rally the unqualified support of all who have at heart the welfare of Canada. A grievance, as was well said yesterday bj the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, because it happens to be the grievance of a minority, should not be lightly discarded or ignored.
