On the contrary, the true basis of strength in a majority lies in the fact that it can dispassionately listen, as it has listened to-day, thank heaven, that it can scrutinize, weigh, solve. It has been stated, I know, that this Parliament should scrupulously avoid dictating its will to any province in matters essentially provincial. Far be it from my mind to dictate to anyone, ot to dictate to any province. Belonging, as I do, to the minority in Canada, need I say that I stand for provincial rights? Historically, traditionally, the Liberal party has always resisted any encroachment on what properly appertains to the provincial domain. But this Parliament, as was admitted a moment ago by the hon. Postmaster General, has never lost its expressive power, nor has any British legislature in the world ever lost its expressive power. My hon. friend said a moment ago that this was not the proper tribunal. I take issue with him on that point. I say that this is the highest court in the land, and that if a subject of His Majesty the King has a legitimate grievance he has the right to ask redress for that grievance before the supplies are voted. That is what the French Canadian minority of the province of Ontario is respectfully doing to-day.
There are questions, I know, more acute in one section of the country than in the other, and because of that very acuteness they affect the well-being, peace and good government of our country. The language issue, unfortunately, is one of these acute questions. It is not a new one, because in a country made up of several nationalities it is liable at times to appear on the surface and bring confusion and misery where peace, harmony, and concord should prevail. It is, unfortunately, a vexed issue, because behind it nestle feelings of pride which tend to embitter and inflame, but I hope that in the few remarks I shall offer the House this evening nothing that I will say may accentuate that bitterness, or arouse acrimony. I fully realize that moderation is a virtue. I will speak this evening the language I would use in the historic city of Quebec, and that I would use to-morrow in the city of Toronto. After all, in this country there is but one constituency for a public man worthy of the name, and that constituency is Canada as a whole.
The bilingual issue has reached such a climax that to-day we are face to face with a condition and not a theory, and I do not

intend to set up a case on behalf of the minority based on any treaty or any statutory enactment. Whatever may be the legal or constitutional aspect of this question, I know full well that a minority must always depend on the good will and forbearance of the majority for the full enjoyment of its rights and privileges. It is, Mr. Speaker, an appeal to reason; nay, more, it is an appeal to fair play, to those generous instincts which have always characterized the British race in its treatment of minorities that I intend to make this evening. The question of whether or not the French were conquered or were ceded does not affect the issue one way or the other. Granted that they were conquered, but I claim that the French were not conquered on the Plains of Abraham. They were conquered in 1774; in 1791; in 1841; they were conquered in 1867, when British diplomacy, wise and strong as it has always been, gave the French Canadian minority all the rights which the British subject enjoys wherever the Union Jack floats. That is your conquest of the French Canadians. The Treaty of Paris, signed in 1763, speaks for itself. The outstanding point remains that there is in Canada today an English-speaking majority and a French-speaking minority. But will you not agree with me, Mr. Speaker, that it is the duty of statesmanship to see that both should learn to appreciate and respect each other? Right here it may not be amiss to recall a proposition laid down by that great British jurist, Lord Mansfield, on the effect of conquest by British arms. Says Lord Mansfield:
The conquered inhabitants once received under the conqueror's protection, become subjects and are universally to be considered in that light, not as enemies or aliens.
The same principle was propounded by Wedderburn, by Marriott, by Thurlow, at the time of the Quebec Act in 1774. That has been the traditional policy of Great Britain in all parts of the world, and I need not say that it is due to that broad, tolerant and fair policy that the British flag to-day floats at the topmast of the British Navy over the Seven Seas, and that Great Britain owns one-sixth of the inhabited globe. A race may be ceded to another race, it may be conquered by force of arms, but every man who has a heart in his breast, every man who has some intelligence in his head-and I am addressing myself to men of the highest intelligence and to men who have hearts in their breasts

-will admit that, ceded or conquered, there are moral frontiers which cannot be overcome by mere force. The language of a race is one of these frontiers. This itself need not be safeguarded by the covenants of a treaty or by statutory enactment. Civilization would be a sham if that were necessary. Why? Because language is part of a man's soul, because there are traditions and ideas binding men to the same language by indissoluble ties, and because it would be cruel to deny,a man the right to speak the language that he learns to lisp at his mother's knee. That language is sweet with the breath and aroma of memories that bring to his heart the joyance of happy tears, that language which exalts, inspires and fills his heart with reverence and faith and heroism that shine as stars in the temple of his race.
During the last half century Germany has vainly tried to eradicate the French language in Alsace-Lorraine. She has vainly tried to suppress Polish in Posen and Danish in Schleswig-Holstein. The Magyars have vainly sought to make their tongue the language of Hungary. But all these attempts have lamentably failed; failed in Alsace, failed in Denmark, failed in Poland, and failed in Hungary. Sir, need I say that the German policy is not of the British ot of the French pattern. When the other day the French army reconquered a considerable portion of the lost province of Ajlsaoe, General Joffre issued a proclamation to th)e Alsatians containing the following ominous words:
Our return is final. You are French forever more; France brings you, with the liberties that she has always represented, respect for your liberty, the liberty of Alsatians, the respect for the traditions of your convictions, of your customs.
Sir, the greatest colonial Empire of any time has been built up by Great Britain, and she has been able to hold that Empire together largely by following the policy of her statesmen, that the traditions, the religious convictions, the civil rights, the customs, and the language of her isubjects shall be respected. It is radically false, I submit, to think that unity of Empire must be based on uniformity of language. Read the history of the world; read the history of the Roman Empire by Gibbon, and you will see that no empire has ever been united by oneness of language. To use the words of a modem writer "a nation, small as dt may be, is a torch and it is important that there should be several luminous centres in the world." I submit

that- the British example demonstrates that diversity of language and of laws, far from being a disintegrating factor, is on the contrary a most healthy and unifying influence. Not to mention India with her mosaic of languages freely taught and freely spoken, take that quaint little island of Malta where Italian is the official language of the courts, and parents have the right to say whether their children shall learn English or ^Italian at the schools. In South Africa, Dutch and English are on an equal footing. It was my privilege in 1910 to be present at .the inaugural ceremonies of the new constitution of South Africa. His Royal Highness the Duke of Connaught, the present Governor General of Canada, w-as there, representing his nephew, His Majesty the King. I well remember the lasting [DOT] impression made upon the minds of every one present when [DOT]the speech from the Throne was read in English and in Dutch, and when the prayers were recited in both languages, just as they are in this House of Commons every day. In Wales a million people speak Welsh, -and 250,000 of them speak Welsh alone. In Ireland the Irish Gaelic is taught in live thousand schools. In the highlands of -Scotland Scotch-Gaelic is the language of a quarter of a million people. In Mauritius, French is the official language. I have in this House friends of Scotch origin, and only yesterday my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) told me that his grandmother spoke not a word of English, but Gaelic only. In the county of Inverness, as in the old Scotch settlements of the county of Gaspe, which I had the honour of representing for fifteen years in this House, I know old Scotchmen who speak the English language with the greatest difficulty, and who have ever been attached to their mother-tongue, the Gaelic language. In the Channel islands things are much like Quebec, except as regards religion. The people in the Channel islands aTe Huguenots, while in Quebec they are Catholics, but both cling to their national traditions, to their language, to their laws, their customs and their usages. But at the same time both are loyal to the British Crown, and both have given evidence of their loyalty. Both are, however, of a conservative frame of mind. A change in the constitution ot an alteration in 10 p.m. the laws is always looked upon with apprehension by the minority. A man who after long struggles
has at last succeeded in obtaining what the Latin poet has so aptly defined " aurea mediocritas " will pause and reflect before he accepts any new proposition presented to him, and in this respect nations are not unlike individuals. Many people I know, honestly believe that there should be uniformity of laws and of language in the Dominion, because forsooth it would be far more practicable. Those who look at such questions from the mere practical point of view are apt to forget that sentiment, after all, is no mean factor in the map of life. I remember when I was a boy at college the first thing I learned in English was " Gray's Elegy in a Churchyard," and the first booklet I was asked to read bore the following suggestive title:	" Put Yourself in his Place."
I am simply asking the majority of my fellow men in this House to put themselves in our place. Our traditions, our laws, out language, constitute the inheritance which was _left to us by our forefathers in 1759. It is a glorious heritage which any man of honour will always treasure. Would not my English speaking friends have less respect for me if I were unfaithful to that sacred trust? For an Englishman, after all, valour is still of value; he will always admire courage, thrift, perseverance displayed by his defeated foe.
Let me remind you, Sir, at this juncture of what happens every day in London, at the very heart of the British Empire. In Downing street, next to the residence of the Fhst Lord of the Treasury, sits the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. This able body of men, some of whom may be classed amongst the greatest jurists in the world, holds periodical sessions to hear the appeals from the several colonies and. dominions. From the Cause List, you will notice that one day an Indian case may be heard and the next day a Canadian case; one day the appeal is from Bengal, the next day it is from Mauritius or Ceylon. Each of these colonies-not to mention the many others-has kept its own laws, and one who is a daily attendant at the sessions, of the Judicial Committee, may listen to very able arguments based on -the common, law, the Roman law, the Dutch law, the Indian law, the Coutume de Paris, or even the Coutume de Normandie, when it is a case from the Channel islands.
It is argued by some usually fair-minded people that once you grant the French language its status in the schools of Ontario, you immediately open the door to similar-

privileges to the foreign-born who seek a *home in Canada. Hence, they say, the imperative necessity of a uni-lingual policy. I hold no brief for the foreign-born, be he Slav, German, Hungarian, Italian, or Greek, he is fully entitled to all the rights of his newly acquired British citizenship. But when an immigrant comes to Canada and settles on the homestead which is freely alloted to him by the bounty of the Canadian Government, he knows that he becomes subject to the laws of the Dominion. He cannot claim special privileges; he knows that there are in Canada but two official languages, the English and French. Surely no one will contend that, as between the immigrant coming from a foreign land and the son of the soil-and we the French Canadians claim to be the sons of the soil for eight, nine and ten generations, the men whose ancestry was here long before the Cession, two hundred and sometimes three hundred years ago-there is no distinction to be drawn. Quebec and Ontario were part of the territory then known under the name of New France, and it is that territory with all its inhabitants which the Treaty of Paris placed Under the domination of Hjs Britannic *Majesty.
As I have already stated, the traditional policy of Great Britain has even been to respect the religion, the civil rights, the usages, the customs, the language of a conquered people. The French Canadian is not an immigrant-I do not use the expression in any offensive sense-and he should not be treated as an immigrant. He does not come on this continent hat in hand, anxious to fit into the new ways of a strange country, ready to cut all bridges behind him, willing to surrender his race individuality by the process of the crucible or the melting pot. Canada is his fatherland; it is not for him an adopted country; it is his country and his only country. Occasionally, the habitant of the province of Quebec or from the French counties of Ontario will emigrate to the New England States to earn money in hard times to pay off a mortgage, but he never bids a final adieu to his farm; his heart remains behind with the long pastures, the bright-hued villages and the tall spires. He naturally clings to the traditions, the ideals, the language, which are so closely associated with the land where his forefathers long before him played such a prominent part.
Right here allow me to say, in order once and for all to answer the very insidious

criticism which is made of the language as spoken by the French Canadian of this country: his language is not a dialect; it is not a patois; it is the language of old France, of France of the I8th century, the language which since the Congress of Vienna has replaced Latin in diplomacy, the language which for centuries was spoken in England, at the Court, in Parliament, the language which in all parts of the civilized world constitutes one of the highest manifestations of humanity. That language has always been respected and recognized by a wise and far-seeing British statesmanship. Evidence of this can be found in a series of Imperial enactments, the latest of which is the British North America Act, of which section 133 reads:
Either the English or the French language may he used by any person in the debates of the Houses of the Parliament of Canada and of the Houses of the Legislature of Quebec and both those languages shall be used in the respective Records and Journals of those Houses.
Mark the words:	either of the two
languages may be used in this House and in the Senate and in both Houses of the Quebec Legislature, and both languages shall be used in the records and the journals. Is it not an elementary proposition that, the English and the French languages, having been thus declared official, in the spirit if not in the letter of the Constitution, it follows that the teaching of both languages was intended to be left free and untrammelled.
Do you look, Sir, for some more evidence of the bilingual complexion of this country? Some thirty-five years ago, when the Marquis of Lome, later on the Duke of Argyll, was Governor General of Canada, he founded the Royal Society of Canada, which has been given an official status by this Parliament. i wish to remind you, Mr. Speaker, and my English-speaking fellow members of the House that there are two sections of that society, the English and the French sections. My hon. friend the member for Kamouraska this afternoon cited another enactment of this Parliament which is evidence that the bilingual complexion of this country is fully recognized. We passed two years ago a new naturalization law in order to meet Imperial requirements. It was sound policy to adopt that legislation. While it was peculiar to Canada a proviso was inserted in that law whereby the English and French languages were considered as test languages for the new-

comers applying for their naturalization papers.
I have read in the press, not without amazement, an assertion to the effect that bilingualism meant French domination. The English-speaking members of this House were solemnly warned not to surrender. Is it possible, Mr. Speaker, that in a country like ours, such warnings should find any echo? Is it possible that any such appeal could be successfully made to a proud and chivalrous race like the English-speaking people? Every French Canadian is anxious that his children should learn English, because English is the language of business. It is the language of the continent of America and no man is fully equipped for the battle of life if he is not conversant with that language. Besides, in a loftier sense the knowledge of English literature is in itself no mean privilege. The idea of French domination is altogether too silly an invention to be seriously entertained. On this continent of America, from the Rio Grande to the polar sea there are 100,000,000 people speaking the English language, and practically the English language only; and as against that immense number of people barely 5,000,000, perhaps less, Louisiana included, use the French language. Can this minority, will this minority ever attempt to dominate the vast majority? The idea is preposterous. No, Mr. Speaker; on this continent, in this country, in this great province of Ontario, the minority could not and would not dominate. It shall not be dpminated, either, if we are all imbued with the spirit of democracy, if we all live up to true British ideals. The French Canadians want equal justice. They want fair treatment, nothing more and nothing less.
Two men have been mentioned in this debate whose name and fame shall ever be remembered in history. They were political opponents, but both were patriots and statesmen. I refer to Sir John A. Macdonald and Edward Blake. They lived at a period when the French population was larger in proportion than it is to-day; when the British isles and the Western States had not poured into the western prairies that steady and healthy stream of immigration which made it necessary in later years to carve two new provinces out of that great lone land. Yet Macdonald and Blake, when the bilingual issue came up before Parliament in 1890, gave utterance
to their views in no huckstering spirit. Let me quote two short sentences from that historic debate in wihich both of them took such a prominent part. The first sentence uttered by Sir John A. Macdonald finds its application in the very Ontario case that we are discussing this evening. True it is that when he spoke he was opposing a Bill which toad been introduced by the late Dalton McCarthy to do away with the French language in the legislative councils of the Northwest Territories. I draw the attention of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and of the Postmaster General to these words of Sir John A. Macdonald. After quoting the resolution which was read a few moments ago by my hon. friend the Postmaster General, which was adopted by Upper Canada in 1793, providing for the translation into French of their Acts for the benefit of the few French settlers in the province, Sir John went on to say:
Are we, one hundred years later, going to be less liberal to our French Canadian fellow-subjects than the few Englishmen, United Empire Loyalists, who settled Ontario? No, Sir. This resolution would oast shame on men who tried to deprive our French friends in the province of Ontario of the privilege given them a hundred years ago by a body of men altogether speaking the English language.
Further on he said, in still more eloquent language:
Are we going to be less liberal? Forbid it, Mr. Speaker. In the name of humanity, in the name of civilization, in the name of the progress of this great country, I appeal to all our friends in this House, without reference to party, to forget what may be an inconvenience when they go back to their constituents on both sides, to forget that for a moment, and to merge everything in the great desire to make Canada, French and English, one people.
I am at a loss to understand the sentiments expressed this afternoon by the right hon. Prime Minister on whose shoulders has fallen the mantle of Sir John A. Macdonald as leader of the Conservative party. Does he believe for one moment that the resolution which is now before the House smacks of coercion? In 1890. the late Dalton McCarthy had introduced a Bill to do away with , the rights of the minority in the councils of the Northwest Territories. Sir John A. Macdonald in hi& answer took the very attitude which is taken today by the leader of the Opposition and by the member for Kamouraska, he appealed to the better instincts of the Canadian majority to treat the French minority in a fair spirit. Not that Sir John A. Macdonald wanted to impose his views upon the people of the Northwest;

not that he wanted to coerce the Executive he simply made the appeal that any true Briton is entitled to make whenever he thinks a wrong is committed.
Sir, thus spoke the old chieftain of the Conservative party, the statesman who built up Confederation, with Cartier and Galt. Listen now to the Hon. Edward Blake, the reader of the Liberal parity-not in 1890, because in 1887 he had himself moved that a man of French birth should succeed him in the leadership of the Liberal party-all honour to his memory for that. Edward Blake, a man whose profound knowledge of the law and constitution made him the peer if not the superior of any man holding a brief before any British court, said:	.
Whether you differ or agree as to what might have been best for the country, in the situation of the country as it stands, I say: No; a thousand times, no to the least effort or proposal to reopen that settled controversy; and I maintain that it is the duty of those who truly regard the progress and the prosperity of Canada, who hope to see it advance in its path towards nationality, to defend the rights of the minorities in this regard, as by law and by convention and by national settlement established. I intend for my part to defend them just as warmly as if I were one of themselves; and I should regard myself as dishonoured and disgraced if I were now to yield to the forces which press me to any other course.
Such was the language of two of the noblest men who ever appeared in public life in this country. But I may be told that what I have just quoted is not relevant to the Ontario case-and remember that when I speak of Ontario I speak with the greatest respect of the Legislature and of the people of Ontario. I am myself a resident of the province of Ontario, and my children I have brought up in that province. Let me state briefly, as I understand it, the grievance of the minority in Ontario. As was stated by previous speakers, long before the Union of 1867 French schools existed in Ontario, and when Confederation took place in 1867 the English minority in Lower Canada was confided by Sir A. T. Galt, by Sir John A. Macdonald, by George Brown, to the care of the Legislature of Quebec in educational matters; and the French-speaking minority of Upper Canada was confided by Sir George Cartier, in educational matters, to the care of the Legislature in Toronto. A denominational system, I may be told, was provided for, not a bilingual system. Is there any one who will seriously contend that Sir John Macdonald, Sir George Cartier and Sir A. T. Galt did not contemplate, in their honesty of purpose, a reciprocity of treat-

ment with regard to both minorities? I have already quoted the weighty words of Sir John Macdonald. Let me read a letter from Mr. Egerton Ryerson, formerly Superintendent of Education, upon that particular point. It is dated Toronto, 24th of April 1857, and was addressed to Messrs Donald McLean, John Cuttenach, Angus McDonnell:
Gentlemen,
I have the honour to state in reply to your letter of the 16th Instant that as the French is the recognized language of the country, as well as the English, it is quite proper and lawful for the Trustees to allow both languages to be taught in their schools to children whose parents may desire them to learn both.
I have the honour to be. Gentlemen,
Tour obedient servant,
(Sigd) E. Ryerson.
Subsequently, and long before Confederation, grants were made,.from time to time, to those bilingual schools. French inspectors were duly appointed to carry out the regulations of the Department of Education with regard to those schools. By regulation 15 the right of the parents to demand that the French or German language be the language of instruction and communication in the schools attended by their children was recognized. I will read, after others, regulation 15, because it cannot be read too often. It is the regulation which we ask the Government of Ontario to reinstate. Let the Department of Education restore that Regulation 15 on behalf of the French as it exists to-day on behalf of the German minority, and the agitation will cehse- and what boon that will be for Canada. That Regulation 15 reads as follows:
In school sections where the French or German language prevails, the trustees may, in addition to the course of study prescribed for public schools, require instruction to be given in reading, grammar and composition to such pupils as are directed by their parents or guardians to study either of these languages and in all such cases the authorized text books in French or German shall be used.
Such was the regulation governing the bilingual schools of Ontario when it was superseded by Regulation 17, a most drastic regulation indeed, which affects the French only and, mark well, not the Germans. I will not say that these bilingual schools were not at times threatened, but be it said to the honour of Sir Oliver Mowat, to the honour of Sir George Ross, they always treated the minority in a broad and generous spirit. The words, from S'ir Oliver Mowat on precisely the same issue have been quoted, but they may well be recalled.
Can my hon. friend tel-l me when Regulation 15 was changed or repealed?
I did not say it was repealed. Regulation 15 exists, but for the German minority only. It has been superseded by Regulation 17 as regards the French schools.

It is on the statutes
just as the hon. gentleman read it.
As regards the French?

Just as you read it.
Do I understand it still remains on the statute book?

My contention is that
it remains on the statute book as regards the German minority, but not as regards the French minority. However, my hon. friend will have occasion in a moment to explain his point. I am proceeding with my remarks.

I want to make that
clear. Does he claim that the wording of Regulation 15 has been changed?

I claim that Regulation 15 does not apply to the French minority as before. It still applies to the German minority, but it does not apply to the French. If I am wrong I wish to be corrected by my hon. friend.
I was saying that on precisely this issue of the English-French schools, as regards the language of communication-and this is the crux of the grievance-Sir Oliver Mowat used the following language:
Our opponents pretend that the Government should insist on all instruction being given to the French children in the English language. No such regulation was suggested by the commissioners, and none such has been made, because such a regulation would be absurd, and, instead of serving the cause of education would often prevent education altogether. How can you teach in a language which the children do not understand?
Sir, Regulation 17, which superseded Regulation 15-and this is the point I wish to emphasize-does away with the system which Sir Oliver Mowat consistently maintained and defended. In other words, Regulation 17, reduced to ite real size and significance, means the gradual elimination of the French language as a language of instruction and communication beyond the First Form, and the suppression of the study of that language, beyond one hour each day, in the other Forms, such study, and the time allowed for it, remember, always and completely subject to the approval and direction of the chief superintendent of education and supervising inspector. Read the Regulation, shorn of its proxility, and any one whose mind is unbiassed will come to the conclusion that it is unworkable and ineffective. This is, put in concrete form, the gist of the complaint of the French minority. Surely three or four men of good will can be found in this Dominion who would sit around a table with the Minister of Education in Toronto, and I venture to say that in half an hour's time the whole controversy would be settled.
The assertion that Regulation 17 is unworkable and ineffective-that is the complaint of the minority'-I do not base on my own judgment, as my hon. Mend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) would infer. It is the conclusion reached by the six inspectors specially appointed by the Ontario Government to report as to the nature and effect of that regulation. The report was unanimous, and here are the findings. I ask any fair-minded gentleman who belongs to the majority in the province o' Ontario to listen to me at this moment because I have reached, I think, the point where the whole difficulty is laid bare. The inspectors appointed by the Government-three were French and three were English-agreed that
The above Regulation 17 has not been effective for the following reasons:	It was taken
to mean that French could not be used as a language of instruction and communication, it was regarded as an attempt to gradually eliminate the French language from the English-French schools.
I now ask were the inspectors unduly pessimistic? Is the FrenclnCanadian minority in Ontario unwarranted in resenting the radical change in the mode of instruction attempted by the Department of Education of Ontario? Let me answer very moderately but very frankly. When it is solemnly resolved by influential public bodies:	" that the use of the French
language in the public and separate schools of Ontario constitutes a grave menace to the integrity of the province, as an Englishspeaking community;" when it is alleged: "that it is not within the power of the provincial Government to compel the observance of the law as long as there is one loophole for the use of the French in the schools when the Government is asked: "to enact such laws and make such amendments to the regulations of the Education Department as will make it unlawful and

impossible for the French language to be used in any of the public or separate schools of the province of Ontario;" when, on the other hand, concurrently with these appeals and as a result of a regulation, most drastic in its terms and character, the number of bilingual schools is limited to those where French has hitherto been a subject of study; when the teaching of French must not exceed one hour, and it may be less; when the language of communication to learn the mother tongue is left at the discretion of the inspector; when the status quo ante .is maintained as regards the German minority-and I do not begrudge the privilege to the German minority, but I claim at least equal rights for the French Canadian minority-and specifically, mercilessly altered as regards the French minority, can anyone, I pray, be surprised if my fellow-countrymen feel aggrieved and molested in what they justly consider is their most sacred privilege?
My right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) this	afternoon	referred to the factthat	he had	learned	French after
he became leader of the Conservative party in the House of Commons. He and I were elected on the same day to this House and I have often told French Canadian audiences in the province f Quebec that I looked upon him as an example of what a British statesman could do in a bilingual country like ours. I have often commended him as I saw him struggling with a language which was not his own, yes, I have often complimented him on the feat, which he had accomplished, of speaking well-yes, very well-the language of my forefathers. I put the question to him, not as representing the minority, but, as I believe he is in spite of his speech this afternoon, as the friend of the minority; I address myself to him as the leader of the Government of this country; as such, I put him above our party quarrels, and I say to him: Take your own experience; you came into this House in 1896 as I did; I could not then speak the English language; you could not speak the French language; if he had been forced to use the French language as the language of communication and of instruction, would he have-attained the knowledge of the French language which he has attained?' And, Mr. Speaker, could I have learned what little English I know if I had been forced to learn it, by setting aside my mother tongue. Mr. Speaker, I say to my hon. friends this is the case; this is the whole question.

This is no vain agitation; it is an appeal for generous treatment made to the majority of this country, and the right hon. gentleman might well rise above party polities and above party success in order to give to the French minority the privileges which it has always enjoyed since this country was ceded to Great Britain by France.
I ask again, Sir, is it to be wondered at that the French Canadians of Ontario feel themselves aggrieved and molested in what they justly consider as their most sacred privilege? No treaty, no statute, no law, can deprive a man of a natural right. If I were not as I am, and as I claim to be, a friend of peace, harmony and concord, I would say to the legislature of the province of Ontario: Maintain regulation 17 and the French will thrive under it; they will pay rates for schools that they cannot and will not send their children to, but they will pay double rates, too, in order to keep for their sons and for their daughters the teaching of the language which they have learned to lisp at their mother's knee. With regard to this question of natural right, the right of a child to learn and to speak the language of his mother, is just as sacred as the duty which devolves upon parents to look after their children, just as sacred as the duty which devolves upon children to support their parents if they are in need.
I may be told, and I believe it is right that I should be told, that the English language was not sufficiently taught in the old bilingual schools, and that this drastic departure was made necessary by that very evasion. I grant that this should not be permitted. But, Mr. Speaker, two wrongs do not make a right. You do not redress a grievance, you do not remedy an abuse, by destroying a privilege. Competent bilingual professors can, however, be found, they can be trained, and their training can be properly supervised and tested, just as their teaching of the pupils can be closely supervised and tested by the proper authority.
Once more, Mr. Speaker, I do not rest my case on- any treaty, on any statute. From my seat in Parliament I rather appeal to the spirit of fair play of my fellowmen of English birth, who are the vast majority in Ontario and in the Dominion of Canada. Let us not forget that it has been decreed by Divine Providence that we, French and English, should live side by side on this half of the North American continent. We

have, therefore, become the trustees of those two proud races which, after centuries of conflict, have become joint partners in Europe in the upbuilding of a higher and nobler civilization. May we not, long after the plains of Abraham, " meet each otner, understand each other, love each other?"
There are, I know, obstacles embedded in the memories of the past, but can they not be overcome by goodwill and mutual forbearance? Is not the history of South Africa an object lesson to us? Less than twenty years ago, that beautiful country was the scene of a deadly struggle-succeeding a turmoil of nearly a century's duration-which threatened to make of the veldt the seat of an everlasting feud. Two proud races were set up the one against the other. Two conflicting ideals were at stake. War with all its bitterness, its vindictiveness, war with all its horrors, raged. It left a land devastated and desolate, a country divided into two camps of victors and vanquished.
To those who judged only by surface indications, to speak of peace might well have seemed a mockery. But there were those who saw deeper and knew that peace had come at last. The brave men who surrendered at Vereeniging kept their selfrespect, but they in return, won the respect, of their adversaries. The war issues were settled without humiliation. England did not fear for her own greatness; the terms made were generous. British statesmanship knows by long experience that a brave foe is usually a staunch friend. Events in South Africa have justified the British in their treatment of the Boers.
I, too, will say to the English-speaking majority of Canada and of the province of Ontario: "Rise up to your own greatness; be generous with the minority; be fair; " and, to repeat the last words of the English captain of the doomed Titanic: " Be British." That is all we ask.
Sir, when after Mons and Charleroi the driven and defeated line of the Allies stood almost under the walls of Paris, when the world expected that the Prussian hordes would soon ride in through its historic gates, thus striking a death blow to the cause of human liberty, there was a halt called by Joffre, and as the grim old soldier stood and watched, men in khaki and other men in dim blue coats suddenly swung out in long lines upon the plain, slowly folding upon Von Kluck's army. As it wheeled eastwards, the bugler blew the charge, .and the English Tommies, for the second time in the history of British arms,
found themselves victorious at Crecy. There in the olden times English knights and French knights had fought and died under the ensigns of St. Denys and St. George. And there again they met in September, 1914, this time side by side as after a long lovers' quarrel to break the Prussian thrust and to once more deliver Christendom and save civilization.
Sir, let us Canadians of French and of English origin take a lesson from that eventful day in the history of mankind. Let us bury the past with its passions, its quarrels, its contention, its miseries. And, exalted by the unique spectacle given to the whole world by both our Mother Countries, let us in common brotherhood and mutual solidarity make of this country what the Fathers of Confederation fervently hoped it would be: a country of equal rights, of toleration, of freedom under the aegis of the British Crown.

Mr. Speaker, at this hour of the night I shall certainly not attempt an oratorical effort even if I were capable of such a thing. But, coming as I do from the province of Ontario, it does not seem unreasonable that I should at least attempt to outline, for the benefit of those who have criticised the legislation and regulations of my province, what I consider to be the law and regulations applicable to education in Ontario. I shall direct my remarks to three aspects of the question: first, the constitutional development of Ontario, and her attitude towards French as a constituted language of instruction in the province. I shall next direct the attention of the House to the development of this bilingual struggle, and then I shall endeavour to explain wherein I think a misapprehension exists in regard to the regulations. In the first place I might say that if anything were necessary to convince me that a resolution of this class should not be introduced into this House it is the great difference of opinion that exists among the speakers who have spoken as to the construction of the regulations, what their meaning is and what the position of the French in the province of Ontario has been and is to-day.	.
The first part of the resolution of the hon. member for Kamouraska says:
It has long been the settled policy of Great Britain whenever a country passed under the sovereignty of the Crown by treaty or otherwise, to respect the religion, usages and language of the inhabitants who thus beqome British subjects.

There is always a danger in stating a tact in the preamble of a resolution. But the resolution is cleverly drawn in this respect, that the preamble is misleading, and to my mind conveys the impression that the religion, usages and language of the original inhabitants of this country were protected and have a right to exist as the religion, usages and language of the province of Ontario. The first speaker this afternoon took the position that it was the inalienable right of every man to have his language, and that it was impossible to take it away from him by legislation, reasoning from that he claimed that it was the inalienable right of the scholar in the province of Ontario to be taught in the French language, and that the province of Ontario had no authority to modify that right. The hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin), being a lawyer, and being more close to Ontario, perhaps appreciated the difficulty into which he was being led and his argument did not go quite so far. But he inferred that the French-Canadian in attendance at the schools in the province of Ontario had by implication certain rights under section 93 and section 133 of the British North America Act. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, in a most wonderful speech of classic eloquence, admitted frankly that this problem must be settled by Ontario. He stated frankly and openly that the predominant right lay with Ontario. Now it is quite impossible to reconcile these three arguments one with another, and I propose briefly, and, jl trust, not to such an extent as to tire the House, to show this House, and perhaps through this House, the country, what Ontario considers to be her position and what she claims is her right.
It has been alleged that by capitulations certain rights and privileges were guaranteed in reference to the language of the French-Canadian population of Ontario. I should like to direct attention first to the Capitulation of Quebec, 8th day of September, 1759. I am quoting from page 6 of the Constitutional Documents of Canada. And let me say. Sir, that if there is one thing I desire to do more than another it is to impress upon this House that Ontario has no desire to act the part of tyrant, and that in speaking as I speak to-night I am only frying to express to this House what I believe to be the true spirit of Ontario, and what I believe her desire and intentions are. Turning to page 6 of the Constitutional Documents of Canada, section 6 of the Articles of Capitulation at Quebec makes

no reference whatever to language, but it does refer to the question of religion, and this is what was demanded:
That the exercise of the Catholic, Apostolic and Roman religion shall he maintained; and that safeguards shall be granted to the houses of the clergy, and to the monasteries, particularly to his Lordship the Bishop of Quebec, who, animated with zeal for religion and charity for the people of his diocese, desires to reside in it constantly, to exercise, freely and with that decency which his character and the sacred offices of the Roman religion require, his episcopal authority in the town of Quebec, whenever he shall think proper, until the possession of Canada shall be decided by a treaty between their most Christian and Britannic Majesties.
And the answer was:
The free exercise of the Roman religion is granted, likewise safeguards to all religious persons, as well as to the Bishop, who shall be at liberty to come and exercise, freely and with decency, the functions of his office, whenever he shall think proper, until the possession of Canada shall have been decided between their Britannic and most Christian Majesties.
That is the only provision I know of in that treaty in reference to language or religion. Turning to the Capitulation of Montreal, which took place on 8th day of September, 1760, approximately a year
11 p.m. later, we find on page 27 of the same book, as follows (Article
41):
The French, Canadians, and Acadians of what state and condition so ever, who shall remain in the colony, shall not be forced to take arms against his most Christian Majesty, or his Allies, directly or indirectly, on any occasion whatsoever; the British Government shall only require of them an exact neutrality.
That is what was demanded, and the answer was:
They become subjects of the King.
Article 42 demanded:
The French and Canadians shall continue to be governed according to the custom of Paris, and the laws and usages established for this country, and they shall not be subject to any other impossibilities, than those which were established under the French dominions.
And the answer was:
Answered by the preceding articles, and particularly by the last.
The reason I made reference to these two capitulations is this. The right hon. leader of the Opposition in addressing the House this afternoon said, in reference to that answer " They become subjects of the King " that the French Canadian subjects of that day had reason to suppose that they would have protection. I suppose he desired this House to infer that protection meant that their usages would be respected,

that their language would be respected, and that their customs would not be disturbed. But if that was the object of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, certainly history does not bear out that conclusion; because His Britannic Majesty, by the proclamation of October 7, 1763, which is quoted on page 118 of the book from which I have been reading, certainly went a long way from protecting what was thought to be the laws and usages of French Canadians of that day, for he ruthlessly east them aside, and by proclamation introduced English Common Law into the province of Quebec. It seems to me that that conclusion cannot be otherwise than reached. And if you admit that the answer " They becoiiX. subjects of the King " entitled His Britan nic Majesty to introduce English Common Law into the province of Quebec, it certainly entitled His Britannic Majesty or any other competent legislative authority to pass'legig-lation affecting the French language in the province or what then constituted Canada. Those who have studied the history of Canada are aware of the discontent that followed in Quebec the proclamation of 1763. They know how the French Canadian, people, in the habit of being governed by the civil law, resented the imposition of the English common law. They know the petitions that went to His Britannic Majesty to restore again to them the law that they had known, and those who have paid attention to the fact are aware that in 1774 the law of France was again restored to Lower Canada. One might naturally ask:	Why
was this done? Was it all done out of kindly consideration for the French Canadian people, or was it done because England wanted to make Lower Canada unsuitable as a colony of Britain? Let me ask you to turn to page 389 of the Constitutional Documents of Canada, where, I think, some very enlightening information may be found. There is a quotation at the bottom of the page taken from one of Cavendish's debates, and this is quoted from one of Lord Wedderburn's speeches:
I think there ought to be no temptation held out to the subjects of England to quit their native soil, to increase colonies at the expense of this country. If persons have gone thither-
That is, Lower Canada.
-in the course of trade, they have gone without any intention of making it their permanent residence; and in that case, it is no more hardship to tell them, " this is the law of the Land "-
That is, the civil law.
-than it would be to say to a man whose affairs induced him to establish himself in Guernsey, or in any other part of North America. With regard to the English who have settled there, their number is very few. They are attached to the country either in point of commercial interest or they are attached to it from the situations they hold under Government. It is one object of this measure that these persons should not settle in Canada. -
Now, the reason I direct the attention of the House to that fact is this, that I want to impress on this country that in 1774, when the Quebec Act was brought into effect, it was not brought into effect with the desire of making Lower Canada a British immigration colony; it was brought into effect to make it a French colony, but part of the British Empire. A change took place, one might almost say, in a night. The war between England and the United States came and went, and men left the United States, preferring their allegiance to the flag to a home in the United States, and they settled in what is now known as Ontario. They were men who spoke the English language. Practically the only French settlements of that day were at the forts of Kingston, Niagara and Sandwich. These men did not know the laws of Paris; they wanted the laws they had known on the other side of the border, and the result was	that the Constitutional Act was passed by which Upper Canada was carved out from what constituted Canada at that time; one of the first Acts of that province was to bring the common law of England into effect, and that law has been .from that time to this the outstanding principle of law governing the province of Ontario.
In all those days nothing was said as to language. Ontario was free to have such language as she wished. It was recognized as an English-speaking colony and Quebec was recognized as a French-speaking colony. We know what history ' tells us subsequently happened. Discord arose not only in the lower province, but in Upper Canada. Lord Durham, astute of mind, far-seeing and tactful, was sent to Canada in the hope of reconciling the two races. His expressive sentence is well known; it is one of the outstanding remarks of history; he said he found "two nations warring in the bosom of a single state," and his solution was a legislative union between Upper and Lower Canada. In 1840 the Union Act came into force, and by that Act it was declared that English should be the



language of debate in that legislature. French was expressly excluded by the Act; but so chivalrous were the people of the joint legislature that in 1848 they passed a resolution asking that French be restored as the language of debate, and their request was acceded to. From 1840 to 1867 things were not just exactly as we might have desired them to be, and in 1867 the best minds in Canada brought about Confederation. Confederation was a compact by which the men in one province conceded certain rights to the men in the other province, and it is a well-known historical fact that Sir John Macdonald desired a legislative union, one central legislative body for the entire country, and I think it is equally well-known that that was found to be impossible because the province of Quebec did not desire such a legislative union.
The British North America Act is the Magna Charts of Canadian liberties; it is the document by which we must judge our rights, and if I read Canadian history aright, my opinion is this, that in these matters of racial and religious difficulties, when they are peculiarly relegated to one province as distinct from the Dominion, the Dominion -is wise if she leaves them alone. This position was the position I took in my very early days in the consideration of public questions when the Jesuits Estates Act stirred this country from one end to the other. I said that was an Act that came within the jurisdiction of the .province of Quebec, and that the Dominion had nothing whatever to say about it.
In 1896 this country was again shaken over another subject of similar character. The right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition said: By "sunny ways" he could find a solution of the difficulty, and in 1896 I refrained from voting for the Conservative candidate in the city of Kingston because I believed that the principle that the right hon. leader of the Opposition then advocated was right, and that hands should be kept off Manitoba, because Manitoba had a right to work but her own educational system free from any interference on the part of the Dominion of Canada. To-night, when this question \s again before the country, I take exactly the same position on general principles that it is wise for the Dominion to be cautious and not start what it may not be able to stop.
Coming to the British North America Act, let us see what the rights of the provinces

are under that Act.' The rights of language are defined by section 133, which reads:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the Houses of the Parliament of Canada and the Houses of the Legislature of Quebec; and both those languages shall be used in the respective Records and Journals of those Houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any Court of Canada established under this Act, and in or from all or any of the Courts of Quebec.
The Acts of the Parliament of Canada and of the Legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
Now, we men from Ontario construe that to mean this, that French is an official language in the courts established under the statutory jurisdiction of the Dominion; that French is an official language in the Parliament of Canada; that English has rights in the province of Quebec; but we say, neither inferentially nor otherwise, does that fact affect, regulate, or control the province of Ontario? It was never contemplated that French should have equal rights in Ontario with the rights accorded to English in the province of Quebec. We take the ground that the fact that right being declared, covers the whole principle of the argument, and that Ontario is free in so far as language goes to make such regulations and to pass such laws as she may desire.
In regard to education, the rights are settled and determined by section 93, which reads as follows:
In and for each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education, subject and according to the following provisions :
1. Nothing in any such law shall prejudicially affect any right or privilege with respect to denominational schools which any class of persons have by law in the province of the Union.
The question is, Sir, what right had any class in the province at the Union? The
section reads as follows:
Nothing in any such law shall prejudicially affecting any right or privilege with respect to-denominational schools which any class of per sons have by law in the province at the Union.
Legislation falling within the prohibition of this" subsection is, of course, ultra vires. The rights and privileges protected are those which any class of persons had by law at the Union with respect to denominational schools. All legislation affecting those rights is not prohibited, but only such legislation as prejudicially -affects them. Whether any given legislation is prejudicial or not is a question of fact to be determined in the particular case. At

the Union the only law of Upper Canada that conferred righte or privileges with regard to denominational schools in Ontario was contained in 26 Victoria, chapter 5. It authorized the voluntary establishment of separate schools by Protestants, by coloured people and by Roman Catholics. The distinguished feature of the Protestant and Roman Catholic separate schools was religious belief. No provision was contained in the Act for the use of any special language. The only schools which were in any sense differentiated by language or race were the schools of the coloured people. There were in Ontario at the Union certain French settlements and also certain German settlements, but neither the French noT the German inhabitants of Ontario were authorized to establish separate schools. Their children attended either the comman, now called public, schools, or the separate schools, as best suited them. But the stathte 26 Victoria, chapter 5, did not, nor did any other law of the province, confer, upon either the French or the German" people any special right or privilege with respect either to the Protestant separate schools or to the Roman Catholic separate schools.
The point that I am endeavouring to make is this: by sections 133 and 93, Ontario has plenary jurisdiction in regard to what language of instruction shall be used in her schools, and she may pass any legislation she desires so long as she does not prejudicially affect the rights that were to be respected pursuant to that Act from which I have just read.
The question naturally arises, has Ontario been reasonable? In regard to the religious aspect of the case, I do not think there is a man in this House who will say that what is commonly known as Protestant Ontario has not been liberal to Roman Catholic Ontario. The rights enjoyed by the Roman Catholic people in Ontario to-day in reference to education are vastly wider than the rights they enjoyed at Confederation. Changed conditions have necessitated new laws: Ontario has met the condition and has been willing to widen the scope and influence and rights of the Roman Catholic population. But in regard to the racial question, in regard to language, a different problem confronts Ontario. We have, as you know, but one system of separate schools, and when you unite in that one school the Irish Roman Catholic and the French Roman Catholic, you must have, if

both are to be adequately taught, two sets of teachers, or a teacher adequately conversant with two languages. Thus you throw a tremendous burden on the taxpayer, and that is the problem Ontario has had to face and is endeavouring to solve.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition referred to-day to what Sir Oliver Mowat did in 1885. That was the first time the question pushed itself into Ontario politics. But Sir Oliver Mowat, a man of tact and shrewdness, pushed it to one side and got it out of the way. He got in the region of Torres Vedras, and was successful. But, as one speaker said this afternoon, you cannot conquer a difficulty by running away from it, and Sir Oliver Mowat, by his speech in 1885, did not conquer the difficulty; he only diverted it. What came to Sir Oliver Mowat in 1885 came much more strongly to the Liberal Government of 1899. I want to read to you, Sir, portions from a certain document published by the Minister of Education for Ontario:
During several years subsequent to 1885 the complaints continued, until in May, 1889, the Hon. G. W. Ross, Minister of Education appointed a Commission of Inquiry, consisting of Messrs. John J. Tilley, Rev. Alfred Reynar and Rev. D. D. McLeod. The reasons given for appointing this commission were that the regulations of the Department of Education required -instructions in English to be given in all public schools, and that the department desired to learn with certainty whether and how far these regulations were complied with in the counties of Prescott, Russell, Essex, Kent and Simcoe or what steps should be taken for the more complete enforcement of the regulations of those counties. The commission, therefore, were specifically directed to consider and report in what way the study of English may be most successfully promoted among those accustomed to the use of the French language in their mother tongue.
The report of the commission declared that progress had been made in the teaching of English in the schools. In very few schools had sufficient attention been given to colloquial exercises, and in 28 schools less than the time prescribed was given in English. The school boards, however, recognized their obligation to obey the law of the province in several particulars, accordingly in 17 schools the results were very satisfactory indeed and in several schools quite equal to the work done in good English schools. In 21 schools fair progress was being made, and in 18 the pupils knew very little English.
That demonstrated, Sir, this fact: that if the regulations were adequately lived up to in the so-called French schools, an adequate education could be had in English and in French. (Reading) f
To meet the deficiencies found to exist the recommendations of the commission included (1) the establishment of a special school for the

training of French teachers in the English language; (2) the holding of special institutes for the benefit of the teacher then in the schools; (3) the calling of the teachers' attention to the necessity of making greater use of the oral or conversational method in teaching English; (4) the introduction of a series of bilingual readers. By the use of such readers, the commission reported, the pupils should in time be sufficiently familiar with English to enable them to receive instructions in this language in the various subjects prescribed. In accordance with these recommendations the department established in 1890, in the village of Plantagenet, a model school for the instruction of teachers in English and French, and a series of bi-lingual readers was introduced. In 1892 the department issued a circular of instructions to teachers in regard to the teaching of English.
In lf!93 the commission of 1889 was re-appointed, with instructions to report especially upon the condition of the schools in Prescott and Russell. They were " to consider and report what progress, if any, has been made in the study of English since the date of the last report." The commission reported in August, 1893, " a decided advance upon the state of things which we found on the occasion of our former visit." The commission also reported:
It only requires that the better methods now being used at the instance of the department be persevered in. In all educational measures time is an essentia! element. And from what has been accomplished in the past four years, the whole benefit of which has not yet been reaped, we may conclude that the continuance of these measures, and the use of such others as may yet be necessary, will give to the people of these counties schools which, as to efficiency, in English, will be quite satisfactory.
The results of the inquiries, with the adoption by the department of the reforms recommended, failed to meet expectations and in August, 1900, the Minister of Education. Hon. R. Har-court, issued a circular to the inspectors directing attention to the needs of the French bilingual schools. "The establishment some years ago", the minister declared, "of an English-French training school at Plantagenet did much towards improving the condition of the schools in the eastern part of Ontario. Advancement has not, however, been as rapid as would be desirable, owing to the difficulty of securing teachers who have the necessary knowledge of both the English and French languages." It was decided, therefore, to establish a course of professional training equivalent to the training given for provincial third class certificates. The minister concluded.
" The regulation requiring that so far as possible all communication between pupils and teacher shall be in English must be carefully observed. There should be a little teaching of English from books until the pupils have gained a fair knowledge of oral English. To this end the teachers should follow the instructions in the circular prepared by the Education Department on the teaching of English."
In 1910 a fresh Commission of Inquiry was appointed, and now I come to a portion of the subject of which I have peculiar knowledge, because I happened to be a member of the Legislature of Ontario at that time. The discussion was not launched

in such a way that it could be stated that it was a matter of religious difference. It was not a matter between the Roman Catholics and the Protestants; it was a difference between Homan Catholics in attendance at the separate schools in the province of Ontario, in the districts into which the French people were coming, and in which, by natural increase, they were increasing. The French Canadians took a predominant control in certain of the schools to such an extent that certain of the Roman Catholic authorities asserted that the English language was suffering in comparison with the French language, and as a result Dr. Merchant was appointed to report. His instructions were:
The investigation should be so conducted as to ascertain whether there has been any departure from the provisions of the Public and Separate Schools Act or any of the Departmental Regulations or circulars affecting such schools, and if so to what extent. As the School Law intended to provide all pupils with a thorough training in English, it is desirable that you ascertain whether, and if so to what extent, the means to attain this end are inadequate or defective.
They laid down the principle that Ontario wanted, every scholar to have an adequate education in English. The right hon. leader of the Opposition agrees *frith that, and I agree with him. It is absolutely essential, if the child in the province of Ontario who speaks French is to havie an equal chance with the child who speaks English, that the French child should' have every opportunity of mastering the English language, and Ontario has never been unwilling to do anything	she could
[DOT]to bring about this result. But before Dr. Merchant reported something occurred. The matter got into the legislature	in 1911.	There	was a
good deal of discussion at the time, a good deal of newspaper controversy, a good deal of national heat; but after giving the matter full consideration, the Legislature of Ontario, on the 22nd day of March, 1911, passed a resolution unanimously and I may say in passing that no French member in the Legislature of Ontario objected to that resolution which reads:
Resolved that the English language shall be the language of instruction and of all communications with the pupils in the public and separate schools of the province except where in the opinion of the Department of Education it is impracticable by reason of pupils not understanding English.
In 1911 I voted for that resolution, and I believe it was sound. As an Englishman I voted for it because I believed that

the children whose mother tongue was French had a right, if they lived in the province of Ontario, to be in their early days educated in that tongue so that they would have a fair chance in the province of Ontario. We did not stand on our strict legal rights in the Legislature. We did not say: if the French come into that province they must learn in the schools we have; but we said to them that in their young days they might be taught in French. We wanted to give them every chance, and that resolution is incorporated in the Legislation of Ontario and stands on the statute book? Could anything be fairer? And yet they say that Ontario is tyrannical, that Ontario is over-bearing. Do they understand the resolutions that prevailed? Do they understand that to-day, in the province of Ontario, if a French child not understanding any English comes into an English settlement and goes to an English school he is entitled to be taught in his mother tongue? Do they understand that we have accorded that right? True it is inconvenient; true it is at times bothersome; but Ontario has not stopped to object to that sort of thing. We welcome them all, we want to give them education because the State, we believe, is better if every pupil has an adequate education. But, as I say, that resolution was passed, and then Dr. Merchant's report came in.
Mr. iMAElCIIL: Did Mr. Racine, who represented Russell, inquire whether the adoption of this resolution would change in any way the standing of the schools of Ontario?
I could not speak positively as to that and therefore I shall say nothing. The resolution passed unanimously.

It is true that before
this resolution was moved in the House there had been one standing on the Order Paper for a long time in the name of the acting-Minister of Education to-day, which went further than this went. It aimed to make the English language the sole language of instruction in the schools, and I understand that this resolution was moved by the late Premier, Sir James Whitney. He amended the resolution which had been proposed by the acting-Minister of Education, and assured the Legislature that it left the law as it was. In fact there is in the Public Schools Act a section which says, in enumerating the duties of teachers, that they shall teach in the English language, except where a child does not understand that language.

Dr. Merchant's report
came in. The right hon. leader of the Opposition this afternoon read at some length, certainly I think to the point, as to what great educationists thought was the proper system of teaching a child in a strange tongue; and the surprising thing is that the very trend of argument of the right hon. leader of the Oppositiop is the thing on which Dr. Merchant relies in the preparation of his report. I wish to read to the House a part of this report to show what the attitude of Ontario towards this whole question of French instruction in Ontario is. It is on page 72 of the report on the condition of English-French schools in Ontario, by Mr. F. W. Merchant, published in 1912. Here is what he says oi^ conditions that promote efficiency:
In some of the schools, the French-speaking children are acquiring a good working knowledge of English, both oral and written. At the same time, they are learning to read and write French, and are being given a satisfactory training in the other branches of a public school education. The success of these schools demonstrates the possibility of carrying out the provisions for education in French-speaking and German-speaking communities if the necessary conditions are observed in the organization and the conduct of the schools.
In the course of the investigation I aimed to inquire into the conditions which appeared to promote efficiency. My conclusions are embodied in the remaining sections of the report:
1.	Language of Instruction. The best results are obtained when the medium of instruction is in the beginning the mother-tongue. Life in the ordinary school is so different from the life of the home that the child on entrance to school finds himself in a strange and perplexing environment. He is bewildered if the language he hears in his lessons has no meaning for him, and for a long time he makes but little progress.
When he appears to learn, he is usually but repeating meaningless words. My conclusions, I find, are in accord with those of others who have investigated the bilingual problem in other parts of the Empire. A discussion on bilingualism was held at the recent Imperial Education Conference, and the question of the medium of instruction received a large share of the attention. While the delegates differed regarding the question of the time when English should be introduced into the course of study, and also regarding the stage at which it should be used continuously as the language of instruction, all were agreed that the child on entrance to school should receive his instruction through the vernacular.
Dr. MacKay, of Nova Scotia, said: " In order to settle the difficulty a commission was appointed-
That was in Nova Scotia.
-and the commission determined, and the Government accepted the determination, that the education of the French-speaking child should commence, and be continued during the first four years in the mother tongue, and French readers were provided for them. While

these French readers were used during the first	four years the	teachers of
these schools were expected to acquaint themselves with the method of teaching English colloquially, and during these four years the children were required to do as much as possible in English so that after the fourth year instruction could go on in English continuously. That is the way the matter stands at present in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I believe the French are pretty well satisfied with it. The children in this way learn English more easily. They can learn written French more rapidly, and that enables them with very little difficulty to commence their studies in English thereafter."
He said four years in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
Yes;
I would be satisfied with four years.

Dr. Parmalee, of Quebec, said: " Our experience abundantly proves that we must first give instruction in the mother tongue. We consider that the instruction must be in the first instance in the mother tongue. The change to a second language comes at a later stage."
Mr. Owen Edwards, in describing the condition of affairs in Wales before the introduction of Welsh as the language of instruction, said: " We thought that the best way of teaching English to a Welsh child would be to make the language and the atmosphere of the school entirely English, and to use Welsh, if at all, for the purpose of absolutely necessary explanations. I can but state the result by quoting from a report of a small committee of teachers of great ability and long experience, a report adopted and published by the Anglesey Education Committee. The infant, as he leaves the infant school, is thus described:	* He reads
words with which he associates no meaning, and is denied access to the written word which would at once call up ideas and stimulate his intelligence. Thus, when he has attained the age of 6 or 7, his book tells him nothing; the language he reads he cannot understand, and the language he understands he cannot read. Then a change came about and Wales allowed the Welsh children to be taught in Welsh in the early days. The report goes on:
Mr. A. T. Davies, in describing the condition of affairs in Wales at the present time, says: " H.M. Inspectors, without exception, reported- I have a sheaf of reports here that I could refer to if necessary-most favourably upon the beneficent operation of the new provisions.
