It may be regarded as typical of numbers of others: ' The introduction of Welsh as the medium of instruction in the infant class has had a most beneficial effect on the whole school; the interest of the scholars is aroused from the beginning, and the older scholars bring to the study of other subjects an alert mind and not a mere memory.' "

When I read that, it seems to me that it must impress the members of this House that we in the Legislature of Ontario in 1911 were right when we said that the French child should be taught in French in its early days. Let me explain what Dr. Merchant's conclusions were as to organization. He says:
The organization which gives, on the whole, the most satisfactory results requires the pupil to remain three years in Form I and two years in Form II, during which time English is made gradually to replace French as the medium of instruction. At the end of this period the most backward pupil should have sufficient command of the language to follow with comparative ease lessons conducted in English.
This organization adds one year to the time commonly taken in English schools to complete the public school course. I am convinced that, considering the additional labour involved in learning a new language, the work cannot be done satisfactorily in a shorter time. In some good schools the extra year is taken in Form III, but, on the whole, pupils make more satisfactory progress when the additional time is spent in the earlier part of the course.
In schools attended by both English-speaking and French-speaking pupils the Englishspeaking pupils are best taught by themselves in Forms I and II. The French-speaking children naturally need, in the beginning, special attention in English not necessary to be given to the English-speaking children, and the separation of classes allows both the Englishspeaking and the French-speaking children to
i-oceed with the least possible loss of time. In such schools the classes are combined with advantage in Form III.
Let me emphasize this fact that when teaching the two languages they had practically to break the classes into two, and have the English in one room and French in the other during the earlier days. He proceeds:
The mixed school offers the French-speaking children the best opportunity of learning English. Not only does this form of organization give them an opportunity of acquiring English through association with the English-speaking pupils on the playground, but it permits of the teaching of English throughout the grades by teachers whose mother-tongue is English and of French by teachers whose mother-tongue is French by a system of exchanges in teachers easy to arrange. Now and then we find a teacher whose mother tongue is English who speaks French perfectly, and one whose mother tongue is French who speaks English perfectly, but instances are rare.
I have read thus far with the purpose of showing that the Education Department of the province of Ontario realized that instruction must be given in French to the French child until he attained a knowledge of English during his early years in school.
Now I come to the regulations, and if the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux), has the control over his party which he

says he has, the whole question is settled, and as the right hon. the leader of the Opposition said to-day, we will rise from this discussion better and wiser men, because clause 12 of section 2 which the ex-Postmaster General said would satisfy the French people has never been repealed and is in effect to-day. The fact is that the men who are criticising these regulations do not understand them. They say that Regulation 17 is a modification of Regulation 12. It is not a modification; it is supplementary thereto. Clause 12 has never been repealed. I read to-night from the School Report of 1915, and this is the regulation that is in effect to-day; it is the law of Ontario to-night. If as the ex-Postmaster General says it meets the requirements of the French people, then the whole subject is settled. We thought there was going to be turmoil, but peace may come out of it. This is the regulation:
12. (2) In school sections where the French or German language prevails, the board may, in addition to the courses of study prescribed herein, require instruction to be given in French or German reading, grammar and composition to such pupils as are directed by their parents or guardians to study either of these languages, and in all such cases the authorized textbooks in French and German shall be used. But nothing herein contained shall be construed to mean that any of the textbooks prescribed for public and separate schools shall be set aside because of the use of the authorized textbooks in French or German.
That regulation is the law in Ontario today, and any school section throughout the province of Ontario where the French or German language prevails, the French people or the German people have a perfect right to have their language taught in their schools. But they must not neglect the English language and the right hon. gentleman the leader of the Opposition says that they should not. That is what we ask in Ontario. We say: when your language prevails in a section, you have a right to teach your language; but having become a majority, you must respect our rights and you must see that our children, and your children as well-because it is as important to us as it is to you that your children should have an adequate education in English. That is the law in Ontario to-day. Let us come to the celebrated Regulation 17.

What does the hon. member mean when he says, where the French language prevails? I will cite the case of Grand Valley, in the country of Glengarry, where 75 per cent of the rate-payers

There were two sets of Regulations 17. This was the regulation passed in 1912 and afterwards thrown out:
1.	There are only two classes of primary schools in Ontario-public schools and separate schools; but, for convenience of reference, the term English-French is applied to those schools of each class in which French is the language of instruction and communication as limited in 3 Cl) below.
'Clause 3 (1) is as follows:
The use of French for Instruction and Communication.
(1) Where necessary in the case of Frenchspeaking pupils, French may be used as the language of instruction and communication; but such use of French shall not be continued beyond Form 1 excepting during the school year of 1912-13, when it may also be used as the language of instruction and communication in the case of pupils beyond Form 1 who, owing to previous defective training are unable to speak and understand the English language.
The original Regulation 17 said that the French language could only be used in form 1 during the school year of 1912-13. But the slightest consideration ought to demonstrate to anybody the impracticability of that regulation. Regulation 17 passed in 1912 was purely temporary in character and in August, 1913, a new circular was prepared and it is called Circu-

lar of Instructions." Here is what the circular said:
There are only two classes of primary schools in Ontario-public schools and separate schools; but, for convenience of reference, the term English-French is applied to those schools of each class annually designated by the minister for inspection as provided in 5 below and in which French is a language of instruction and communication as limited In 3 (1) below.
Now, observe what was the intent of that instruction. As I have endeavoured to point out, the province of Ontario says that every child is entitled to an English education. The province of Ontario, tor l.< or 20 years, had been wrestling with this problem of bilingual education. It could not be solved by leaving it to the school boards to regulate each local situation. First, the minister said:	I am going to
take control of these recalcitrant schools and I am going to put them in a class by themselves. If every school will handle the teaching of English as it should be handled in the primary grade; if every school board will see that English is adequately and emciently taught, it may pursue it own course, but if any school board wu. not do that, then I am going to take the administration of that school under my control. That is what Regulation 17 does and it is in that respect that it modifies what is sometimes called Regulation 15. Regulation 17 simply enables the Minister of Education to say: If the school board in a certain school section will not see that English is properly taught, then I am going to see that it is done by virtue of the inspection that the section' provides for. The school may come under Regulation 17 today and not be under it next year. The School Board may observe the provisions of the law. The result will be that the minister will not have again to put the school under Regulation 17.
The sense of responsibility may make the School Board come to the conclusion that it will , observe the law of Ontario and see that the children get an adequate education in( English and, observing the law, and the minister being satisfied of their good faith, the school goes out of Regulation 17 and the general law applies. It is purely a supplementary system for controlling those who are not willing to accept what the province of Ontario considers the ideal educational system. That is all it is. It does not take from the French people anything; in fact, it gives them something that they have not legally aad. Accentuation has been put on the word "hitherto." That word gives the

French in Ontario more than they had before, because there are schools now under this Regulation 17 in which French was' illegally taught before they were brought under the regulation. It was illegally taught because French was not the language that prevailed in the section in which the school was situated. But, the province of Ontario was.so fair that they said: If you have taught French, we are not going to take the right from you and you can have French taught after you are put under Regulation 17.
Men from Ontario feel ruffled at times because we have sent our boys to avenge Catholic Belgium and maintain the status of France and we have been told by French Canadian newspapers, and it has been said by members of this House, that because there were differences on this educational problem, certain of the French Canadian people would not enlist. Certain of the leaders of French Canadian thought, to whom my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition did not refer this afternoon in complimentary terms, have induced the people to hold back when the men of Ontario were going. I want to say in all sincerity in this House to-night, and I trust I speak as a moderate man, that when this war is over, when victory perches on our banners, do not let the men who induced the French Canadians not to enlist, resent it if certain elements in the province of Ontario take theiir race at the value set upon it by their leaders. We in Ontario have sent our men overseas to protect Catholic Belgium in her agony, and to maintain France in her integrity, and we do not want to be told that ether men have not enlisted because they cannot have exactly what they want in Ontario. We in Ontario love our language, we demand our right to' have our children educated in the English tongue. It may not be as soft, as gentle, as smooth a language as the French language, but any man who associates it with his civilization, who knows it in his literature, regards it just as dearly a6 the French Canadian regards his tongue. We in Ontario require that every child gets a good education in English and if our French Canadian citizens will co-operate with us in this, then the province of Ontario will have no grudge against the French. But I say here, with every conviction and in all sincerity, that Ontario is determined that English must be the language of her schools. In the early days we are quite walling that the

French child should be taught in the French language, but we are determined that every child shall have an adequate education in English while at the same time we do not begrudge the, French child the privileges of our schools in order that he may be educated to take his place in this province and in this country.
